structure.title: SUSTAINABILITY STATEMENT OF THE PKO BANK POLSKI S.A. GROUP FOR 2024
structure.heading: 13. SUSTAINABILITY STATEMENT OF THE PKO BANK POLSKI S.A. GROUP FOR 2024
structure.start_phrase: The information, data and ratios and statements contained in the statement relate to the PKO Bank Polski S.A Group, i.e. the parent company PKO Bank Polski S.A together with its consolidated subsidiaries, unless otherwise indicated.
structure.summary:
- Capital markets and funding events:
  - A bond issue with variable interest (quarterly payments) received an A3 rating from Moody’s; admitted to trading on the Luxembourg Stock Exchange, with an intention to list in Warsaw.
  - On 20 Feb 2025, PKO Bank Hipoteczny S.A. issued PLN 800 million mortgage covered bonds (series 15), dated 27 Feb 2025, maturing 27 Feb 2029, at 3M WIBOR + 0.80 bps.

- Credit risk mitigation:
  - On 30 Jan 2025, the Bank amended an unfunded credit protection (CRR) guarantee on a selected corporate receivables portfolio: total covered debt portfolio PLN 16,886 million split into Portfolio A (bonds) PLN 2,365 million with 100% coverage and Portfolio B (other receivables) PLN 14,521 million with 80% coverage; the Guarantee cap remains PLN 13,982 million.

- Corporate event:
  - On 14 Feb 2025, BSafer sp. z o.o. (a joint venture of PKO VC–fizan within the Group) filed for bankruptcy due to insolvency.

- Sustainability Statement (2024) – basis of preparation:
  - Scope: PKO Bank Polski S.A. Group (parent plus 36 consolidated subsidiaries as of 31 Dec 2024), aligned with the 2024 consolidated financial statements’ consolidation scope.
  - Reporting obligation: only the Bank is required to report for 2024; disclosures cover the value chain upstream and downstream, including Scope 3 GHG emissions and consumer/end‑user matters.
  - Completeness and transparency: no use of options to omit information on IP/know‑how/innovation or to withhold information on upcoming/negotiated matters.
  - Policy reporting approach: policies presented on a consolidated basis; where no Group policy exists, the Bank’s policies are shown as a baseline for future Group-level adoption; subsidiaries’ own policies are not detailed as no subsidiary reported entity‑specific IROs or has a 2024 sustainability reporting obligation.
  - Objectives: disclosed where defined for Group-level policies.
  - Governance of internal regulations: Management Board resolutions include responsibility for implementation; for Procedures/Principles/Decisions, the responsible organizational level is indicated; policies/regulations apply without exclusions unless specified.
  - Reporting period and assurance: annual report for 1 Jan–31 Dec 2024; no indicators with high measurement uncertainty identified; indicators not subject to separate attestation beyond the sustainability statement’s attestation.
  - Cross-referencing: the Group does not identify information included by reference to other parts of the Directors’ Report.

nodes.title: GENERAL INFORMATION
nodes.heading: 13.1 GENERAL INFORMATION
nodes.start_phrase: The information, data and ratios and statements contained in the statement relate to the PKO Bank Polski S.A Group, i.e. the parent company PKO Bank Polski S.A together with its consolidated subsidiaries, unless otherwise indicated.
nodes.summary:
- Post-balance-sheet events and capital market actions:
  - Moody’s assigned an A3 rating to a Bank bond issue; the bonds were admitted to trading on the Luxembourg Stock Exchange, with plans to list them on the regulated market in Warsaw.
  - An annex to an unfunded credit protection guarantee (under CRR) was executed on 30 Jan 2025: the covered Group debt portfolio totals PLN 16,886m, split into Portfolio A (bonds) PLN 2,365m with 100% coverage and Portfolio B (other receivables) PLN 14,521m with 80% coverage; the maximum guarantee amount remains PLN 13,982m.
  - BSafer sp. z o.o. (a joint venture of PKO VC-fizan within the Group) filed for bankruptcy on 14 Feb 2025 due to insolvency.
  - PKO Bank Hipoteczny S.A. conducted a subscription for series 15 mortgage covered bonds of PLN 800m, issued on 27 Feb 2025 and maturing on 27 Feb 2029, bearing interest at 3M WIBOR plus a 0.80 bps margin.

- Sustainability Statement (2024) – basis of preparation and scope:
  - Covers PKO Bank Polski S.A. Group (parent plus 36 consolidated subsidiaries as at 31 Dec 2024), with the same consolidation scope as the 2024 consolidated financial statements; only the Bank is legally required to report for 2024.
  - Includes upstream and downstream value chain considerations, Scope 3 greenhouse gas emissions, and consumer/end‑user issues.
  - No use of omissions for intellectual property/know‑how/innovation or withholding of information about upcoming events or negotiations.
  - Policies are presented on a consolidated basis; where Group policies are absent, Bank policies are used as a starting point for Group-level regulation and may be transferred to subsidiaries. Subsidiary-specific policies are not detailed, as no entity reported unique impacts, risks, or opportunities, nor separate reporting obligations.
  - Objectives are disclosed where defined at Group policy level. The Management Board bears responsibility for policy implementation; the organizational level for Procedures/Principles/Decisions is specified. Policies/internal regulations apply without exclusions unless stated.
  - Report prepared annually for 1 Jan–31 Dec 2024; no indicators with high measurement uncertainty; indicators are not subject to external attestation beyond the sustainability statement’s own attestation.
  - The Group does not rely on cross-references to other parts of the Directors’ Report.

nodes.title: BASIS FOR THE PREPARATION OF THE SUSTAINABILITY STATEMENT [BP-1, BP-2]
nodes.heading: BASIS FOR THE PREPARATION OF THE SUSTAINABILITY STATEMENT [BP-1, BP-2]
nodes.start_phrase: The information, data and ratios and statements contained in the statement relate to the PKO Bank Polski S.A Group, i.e. the parent company PKO Bank Polski S.A together with its consolidated subsidiaries, unless otherwise indicated.
nodes.summary:
- Capital markets activities:
  - Variable-rate bond issue with quarterly payments rated A3 by Moody’s, admitted to trading on the Luxembourg Stock Exchange; intention to list also on the regulated market in Warsaw.
  - PKO Bank Hipoteczny S.A. issued series 15 mortgage covered bonds: PLN 800 million, issue date 27 Feb 2025, maturity 27 Feb 2029, floating 3M WIBOR + 0.80 bps.

- Significant post–balance sheet events (2025):
  - 30 Jan: Annex to an unfunded credit protection guarantee (CRR) for a Group corporate credit portfolio. Total portfolio PLN 16,886 million: Portfolio A (bonds) PLN 2,365 million at 100% coverage; Portfolio B (other receivables) PLN 14,521 million at 80% coverage; maximum guarantee amount unchanged at PLN 13,982 million.
  - 14 Feb: BSafer sp. z o.o. (a PKO VC-fizan joint venture within the Group) filed for bankruptcy due to insolvency.

- Sustainability Statement for 2024 – scope and methodology:
  - Applies to PKO Bank Polski S.A. Group (parent plus 36 consolidated subsidiaries as at 31 Dec 2024), with consolidation scope aligned to the 2024 consolidated financial statements.
  - Only the parent bank is legally obliged to report for 2024, but disclosures cover the Group’s value chain (upstream and downstream), Scope 3 GHG emissions, and consumer/end-user matters.
  - No omission of information related to intellectual property, know-how, innovation, or withholding of information on upcoming events/negotiations.
  - Policies are presented on a consolidated basis; where no Group policy exists, the Bank’s policy is presented; subsidiaries’ own policies are not detailed as no subsidiary reported entity-specific impacts/risks/opportunities or separate reporting obligations. Objectives are disclosed where defined at Group level.
  - Governance of policies: adopted by Management Board; procedures/principles/decisions specify implementing organizational levels; no exclusions unless explicitly stated.
  - Reporting period 1 Jan–31 Dec 2024; no indicators with high measurement uncertainty; indicators attested only through the sustainability statement attestation; no cross-referencing to other report sections.

- Governance structure and composition:
  - Management Board: 7 executives (6 men, 1 woman); women’s share 17% at year-end (average 11% in 2024). Clear division of responsibilities across strategy, internal audit, security, compliance/conduct/reputation risk, legal, HR, communications/marketing, corporate governance; retail and corporate banking (retail products, investment/insurance offering design, sales/service to individuals and companies); corporate and investment banking (investment banking, custody, treasury products, corporate/public sector client offering and sales); finance and accounting (macroeconomics, planning/controlling, accounting/reporting, tax, sustainability); administration (property, procurement); operations and international banking (operations, customer advocacy, international/institutional clients, remote channels, product administration, cash management); technology (IT); risk management (all risks except compliance/conduct/reputation; restructuring and recovery).
  - Competency and suitability: periodic individual and collective assessments; PFSA approval required for the President and the risk-management Board member.
  - Supervisory Board: 8 non-executive, all independent; women’s share 33% at year-end (average 47% in 2024). Members meet qualifications for companies with State Treasury participation; backgrounds in academia, business, and audit-advisory, with extensive supervisory and senior banking/audit experience.

nodes.title: THE ROLE OF THE ADMINISTRATIVE, MANAGEMENT AND SUPERVISORY BODIES [GOV-1]
nodes.heading: THE ROLE OF THE ADMIN ISTRATIVE , MANAGEMENT AND SUPE RVISORY BODIES [GOV-1]
nodes.start_phrase: As of 31 December 2024, the Management Board of PKO Bank Polski S.A. consisted of seven executive members: six men and one woman.
nodes.summary:
- Governance structure and composition:
  - As of 31 December 2024, the Management Board had seven executives (6 men, 1 woman; 17% women at year-end, avg. 11% in 2024). The Supervisory Board had eight non-executive, all independent members (33% women at year-end, avg. 47% in 2024).
  - Clear internal division of Management Board responsibilities across strategy, audit, security, compliance/conduct/reputation risk, legal, HR, marketing/communications, retail/corporate banking, corporate & investment banking, finance/accounting/tax/sustainable development, administration, operations/international banking/remote channels, technology, and risk management (all risks except compliance/conduct/reputation; includes restructuring and recoveries).
  - Board members have senior banking/financial market experience; periodic individual and collective suitability assessments; appointment of the President and the risk-management Board member requires Polish FSA approval.
  - Supervisory Board members meet State Treasury company criteria and bring academic, business, and audit/banking oversight experience.
  - Diversity snapshot (31 Dec 2024): Supervisory Board 2 women/6 men; Management Board 1 woman/6 men; Material Risk Takers 18 women/66 men. Age: no members below 30; Supervisory Board mostly 50+; Management Board balanced between 30–50 and 50+; MRTs mostly 30–50.

- Sustainability governance and competencies:
  - ESG knowledge development guided by regulations, needs assessments, mandatory training reports, inspections, and role/qualification analyses.
  - ESG knowledge and the ability to manage ESG risk are verification criteria in preliminary and annual suitability assessments (individual and collective) for the Management and Supervisory Boards.
  - Performance reviews include monitoring non-financial indicators and ESG goals, management objectives tied to strategy, and organizational impacts on stakeholders and society.
  - 2024 workshops for the Sustainable Development Committee (SDC), Management Board, and Supervisory Board covered climate competitiveness, carbon footprints, supply-chain mechanisms, financial institution requirements, climate strategy integration, Poland’s energy mix, evolving standards (SBTi, CDP, TCFD), and footprint reduction methods.

- Sustainable Development Committee (SDC):
  - Primary advisory body to the Management Board on significant impacts, risks, and opportunities (IROs); oversees sustainability and energy transition initiatives; supports priority-setting, action plans, goals, and the sustainability management framework.
  - Meets at least quarterly; chaired by the VP for Finance and Accounting with the VP for Risk as deputy; two Management Board members participate, and the Board reviews minutes and reports.
  - Subordinate to the Management Board, which may amend its mandate; coordinates with other committees; exclusions include matters under the Credit Committee (e.g., limits and credit policies).
  - Recommends objectives, action plans, and timelines based on IRO analyses; monitors progress, accepts reports, and issues recommendations to the Management Board (and, when needed, the Supervisory Board).

- Information to governing bodies (GOV-2):
  - 2024: first ESRS-aligned double materiality analysis completed; future analyses to be performed when new IRO indicators emerge.
  - Management Board approved the list of significant IROs, integrated into strategy oversight via the SDC and Strategy Committee.
  - Key IROs overseen by SDC:
    - Impacts: client-portfolio GHG emissions; financing high-CO2 sectors; green fleet financing; reduced energy dependence; improved competitiveness.
    - Risks: rising investment needs in sustainable energy/efficiency; new building energy regulations; volatility in carbon allowance prices.
    - Opportunities: energy storage, energy infrastructure investment, CO2-limiting regulations, demand for CO2-reduction financing, green bonds growth, low-emission transport, renewables in construction, sustainable energy demand, EV charging infrastructure.

- Incentives and remuneration integration (GOV-3):
  - Remuneration policies for Supervisory and Management Boards and Material Risk Takers align with social interest, environmental protection, and mitigation of negative social impacts, and link to strategy execution.
  - Variable pay for Management Board members is tied to achieving ESG goals embedded in the Bank’s Strategy via KPIs for strategic initiatives; KPI outcomes affect performance bonuses.

nodes.title: INFORMATION PROVIDED TO ADMINISTRATIVE, MANAGEMENT AND SUPERVISORY BODIES [GOV-2]
nodes.heading: INFORMATION PROVIDED TO ADMINISTRATIVE , MANAGEMENT AND SUPE RVISORY BODIES [GOV-2]
nodes.start_phrase: In 2024, the Bank conducted its first double materiality analysis in accordance with the European Sust ainability Reporting Standards (ESRS) and due diligence principles.
nodes.summary:
- Outlines the role of the Sustainable Development Committee (SDC) in PKO Bank Polski’s governance, including supporting the Management Board in setting ESG priorities, action plans, goals, and timelines, and monitoring progress through required reports and recommendations.
- Clarifies competency boundaries: SDC excludes matters under the Bank’s Credit Committee (e.g., credit limits and policies) when applying ESG indicators to products and services.
- Describes information flows to administrative, management, and supervisory bodies, noting the Bank’s first double materiality analysis conducted in 2024 under ESRS and due diligence principles, with future analyses triggered by new indicators of significant impacts, risks, and opportunities (IROs).
- States that the Management Board approved the list of significant IROs, with oversight performed by the SDC and the Strategy Committee.
- Summarizes key IROs:
  - Impacts: client portfolio greenhouse gas emissions, financing high-CO2 companies, green fleet financing, reduced energy dependence, improved competitiveness.
  - Risks: higher investment needs in sustainable energy/efficiency, new building energy consumption regulations, sudden rises in carbon allowance prices.
  - Opportunities: energy storage, energy infrastructure investment, tighter CO2 regulations, demand for CO2-reduction financial services, growth of green bonds, low-emission public transport and economy, renewable energy in construction, rising demand for sustainable energy, EV charging infrastructure development.
- Notes governance practice whereby, due to Management Board representation on the SDC, most decisions are taken at Committee level; only exceptional matters (e.g., acceptance of double materiality results) are escalated to the Management Board and Supervisory Board.
- Explains integration of sustainability into incentive schemes: remuneration policies require Management Board goals to reflect social interest, environmental protection, and mitigation of negative social impacts, aligned with Bank and Group strategy.
- Confirms variable remuneration for Management Board members is linked to ESG objectives embedded in strategic initiative KPIs, with KPI performance influencing bonuses.

nodes.title: INTEGRATION OF SUSTAINABILITY-RELATED PERFORMANCE IN INCENTIVE SCHEMES [GOV-3]
nodes.heading: INTEGRATION OF SUSTAI NABILITY -RELATED PERFORMANCE IN INCENTIVE SCHEMES [GOV-3]
nodes.start_phrase: The incentive schemes and remuneration principles for members of the governing, management, and supervisory bodies are based on the "Remuneration Policy for Members of the Supervisory Board and Management Board of Powszechna Kasa Oszczędności Banku Polskie go S.A." and the "Principles of Remuneration for Employees Whose Activities Have a Significant Impact on the Bank's Risk Profile."
nodes.summary:
- Governance framework: The Sustainable Development Committee supports the Management Board in setting sustainability priorities, action plans, goals, and implementation timelines. Its remit excludes matters reserved for the Credit Committee (e.g., limits and credit policies). It reviews progress, accepts reports/statements, and can issue recommendations; with two Management Board members on the Committee, most decisions are taken at Committee level, with only exceptional escalations (e.g., approval of double materiality results) to the Management Board/Supervisory Board.
- Information to governing bodies and double materiality: In 2024 the Bank conducted its first ESRS-aligned double materiality analysis following due diligence principles. Significant impacts, risks, and opportunities (IROs) were approved by the Management Board and are overseen within the Sustainable Development and Strategy Committees. Future analyses will be refreshed when new IRO indicators arise.
- Key IROs overseen:
  - Impacts: Client portfolio GHG emissions; financing to high-CO2 companies; green financing for fleet modernization; potential energy dependence reduction; competitiveness improvements.
  - Risks: Rising investment needs in sustainable energy/efficiency; new building energy-consumption regulations; sharp increases in carbon allowance prices.
  - Opportunities: Energy storage development; energy infrastructure investments; tighter CO2 regulations; growing demand for CO2-reduction finance; expansion of the green bond market; low-emission public transport; low-emission economy emphasis; renewable energy in construction; sustainable energy demand; EV charging infrastructure.
- Integration of sustainability into remuneration (incentives):
  - Management Board: Variable pay tied to achieving ESG-related strategic KPIs; goals must reflect social interest, environmental protection, and minimizing negative social impacts; decarbonization goals embedded in two strategic programs; in 2024, a diversity KPI (share of women in roles with significant risk impact) accounted for 10% as a corrective indicator. Exact climate-linked pay share cannot be isolated.
  - Supervisory Board: Fixed remuneration only; assesses Management Board effectiveness on ESG via performance approvals.
  - Group companies: No direct pay link for boards/supervisory boards, but management goals should align with Group ESG targets for 2025–2027.
  - Material Risk Takers (including Management Board): MbO-based goals with risk-sensitive criteria; bonuses adjustable per the Annual Note, with upward adjustments capped at 100% of fixed pay. Payouts for Management Board contingent on General Meeting approval of financials, discharge, and compliance with public/state property management requirements (incl. “chimney act”). Variable pay may be reduced for misconduct, legal/standard breaches, poor task performance, or inappropriate behavior.
  - Approval of schemes: Management Board remuneration frameworks approved by the General Meeting and Supervisory Board; MRT principles approved by the Bank’s Management Board.
- Employee representation: Employees are represented by trade unions, the Bank Employee Council, and Social Labour Inspection; the Bank does not impede participation and cooperates per applicable regulations.
- Due diligence statement: The Group applies ongoing, proactive due diligence to identify, prevent, and mitigate negative impacts; process elements are detailed throughout the report.

nodes.title: EMPLOYEE REPRESENTATION [GOV-1]
nodes.heading: EMPLOYEE REPRESENTATI ON [GOV-1]
nodes.start_phrase: Employees are represented at the Bank by the trade unions, the Bank Employee Council and the Social Labour Inspection.
nodes.summary:
- Supervisory Board members receive only fixed remuneration and oversee sustainability governance by assessing the Management Board’s effectiveness through approval of performance reviews, linking indirectly to climate governance.
- Remuneration policy does not directly tie board and supervisory board pay to sustainability metrics, but management goals are aligned with the Bank’s 2025–2027 ESG Strategy.
- In 2024, Management Board evaluation included a sustainability metric on the share of women in roles significantly affecting the Bank’s risk profile; this accounts for 10% of the Bank’s score used to adjust variable remuneration.
- Decarbonisation objectives are embedded in two strategic programmes, though the portion of remuneration tied specifically to climate goals cannot be isolated.
- Variable pay for Material Risk Takers (MRTs), including Management Board members, is based on management by objectives (MbO) with risk-sensitive criteria reflecting the economic cycle and risk profile.
- Bonuses for MRTs may be adjusted based on the Bank’s Annual Note, with upward adjustments capped at 100% of fixed remuneration.
- Payment of Management Board bonuses requires General Meeting approval of financial statements, discharge of Board members, and achievement of management goals, including compliance with public regulations on state property management and the “chimney act.”
- Variable remuneration can be reduced for violations of duties, legal non-compliance, poor task performance, customer service breaches, or behavior infringing social cohabitation principles.
- Incentive scheme governance: for the Management Board, policies are set by the General Meeting and Supervisory Board; for MRT employees, principles are set by the Management Board.
- Employee representation is ensured via trade unions, the Bank Employee Council, and Social Labour Inspection, with the employer supporting participation and cooperation per regulations.
- Due diligence is applied as a continuous, proactive process to identify, prevent, or mitigate negative impacts, with detailed elements described elsewhere in the report.

nodes.title: STATEMENT ON DUE DILIGENCE [GOV-4]
nodes.heading: STATEMENT ON DUE DILI GENCE [GOV-4]
nodes.start_phrase: The Bank’s Group applies the principle of due diligence through a continuous and proactive process aimed at identifying negative impacts and making decisions to exclude or reduce them.
nodes.summary:
- Governance and remuneration in relation to sustainability:
  - Supervisory Board members receive fixed remuneration only; they assess Management Board effectiveness on ESG by approving performance reviews, indirectly contributing to climate governance.
  - Group remuneration policies do not directly tie board pay to sustainability; however, management goals across the Group are expected to support ESG objectives in the 2025–2027 Strategy.
  - In 2024, Management Board evaluation included a sustainability metric: the share of women in roles significantly affecting the Bank’s risk profile (10% weighting as a corrective indicator for variable pay).
  - Strategic programme goals, including decarbonisation in two programmes, inform performance notes; the climate-linked share of remuneration cannot be isolated.
  - Variable pay for Material Risk Takers (MRTs), including Management Board members, is set via Management by Objectives with risk-sensitive criteria; potential upward adjustment capped at 100% of fixed pay and contingent on GM approval of financials, discharge, and compliance with state property and “chimney act” requirements.
  - Variable components may be reduced for misconduct, legal non-compliance, poor task performance, or inappropriate behavior.
  - Incentive scheme governance: GM and Supervisory Board approve policies for Management Board; Management Board approves MRT remuneration principles for employees.

- Employee representation:
  - Employees are represented by trade unions, the Bank Employee Council, and Social Labour Inspection; the Bank does not restrict participation and cooperates per regulations, with further detail referenced in the workforce section.

- Due diligence statement:
  - The Group applies a continuous, proactive due diligence process to identify, prevent, and mitigate negative impacts.
  - Core elements of due diligence (governance embedding, stakeholder engagement, impact identification, mitigation actions, and effectiveness tracking) are mapped to dedicated chapters/ESRS references in the report.

- Risk management and internal controls:
  - An internal control system supports effective operations, reliable reporting, risk management compliance, and legal/regulatory adherence, including the reporting process.
  - Key non-compliance risks in external reporting (deadlines, data quality, classification, missing disclosures) are mitigated via partial automation, verification, audits, controls, and authorizations; overall risk assessed as moderate.
  - Work is in progress to incorporate sustainability reporting risk into the reporting process.
  - No dedicated integration of sustainability-reporting control findings into internal functions yet; 2025 internal audit plan excludes sustainability reporting, with potential inclusion in the 2026–2028 strategic plan based on risk assessment.
  - Internal audit results are reported to the Management Board, Audit Committee, Supervisory Board, and the PFSA Office (for the Bank and Bank Hipoteczny).

- Double materiality assessment (2024):
  - First ESRS-aligned double materiality assessment conducted with external experts at Group and subsidiary levels, covering own activities and exposures (asset structure, sectoral credit exposure, geographic distribution).
  - Broad stakeholder engagement via a survey (targeted 330,483 stakeholders) from 13 Aug to 20 Sep 2024, including subsidiaries, employees, external stakeholders, and experts.
  - Comprehensive scoping produced initial lists of 245 impacts, 165 risks, and 119 opportunities, developed with input from experts across key Bank and subsidiary departments.

nodes.title: RISK MANAGEMENT AND INTERNAL CONTROLS [GOV-5]
nodes.heading: RISK MANAGEMENT AND I NTERNAL CONTROLS [GOV-5]
nodes.start_phrase: The Bank Group has an internal control system that is adapted to the type and scale of its business.
nodes.summary:
- Outlines the core due diligence elements in the Sustainability Statement, including governance/strategy integration, stakeholder engagement, identification and assessment of adverse impacts, actions to address them, and tracking/communication, with references to relevant ESRS disclosures.
- Describes the Group’s internal control system tailored to its business scale, ensuring operational effectiveness, reliable reporting, and compliance with laws, internal regulations, supervisory recommendations, and market standards.
- Details the external reporting process and key non-compliance risks (missed statutory deadlines, data quality issues, misclassification, missing disclosures), along with mitigation measures such as partial automation, ongoing verification, audits, controls, and report authorization; overall risk assessed as moderate.
- Notes ongoing work to incorporate sustainability reporting risks into the reporting-control framework; currently no dedicated integration of sustainability reporting control findings into internal functions.
- States that the 2025 internal audit plan excludes a sustainability reporting audit; potential inclusion in the 2026–2028 strategic audit plan will depend on future analysis and risk assessment. Audit results are regularly submitted to governing bodies and, for the Bank and Bank Hipoteczny, to the PFSA Office.
- Presents the Group’s first double materiality assessment (2024), aligned with ESRS, conducted at Group and subsidiary levels, covering own activities, asset structure, sectoral credit exposures, and geographic portfolio distribution, supported by external experts.
- Explains stakeholder engagement via a large-scale survey (Aug 13–Sep 20, 2024) targeting 330,483 stakeholders, including subsidiaries’ representatives, employees, external stakeholders, and experts, to validate key impact and financial materiality topics.
- Reports the development of an initial universe of 245 impacts, 165 risks, and 119 opportunities, assessed by experts from key Bank departments and subsidiaries with external support, leading into impact materiality analysis.

nodes.title: DOUBLE MATERIALITY ASSESSMENT [IRO-1, IRO-2]
nodes.heading: DOUBLE MATERIALITY AS SESSMENT [IRO-1, IRO -2]
nodes.start_phrase: In 2024, the Bank's Group conducted its first double materiality assessment aime d at identifying key issues related to impacts, risks, and opportunities related to sustainable development.
nodes.summary:
- Context: Excerpt from PKO Bank Polski S.A. Group Director’s Report 2024, focusing on the Sustainability Statement’s due diligence chapter, risk management and internal controls, and the first double materiality assessment.
- Due diligence core elements: 
  - Embedding due diligence in governance, strategy, and the business model.
  - Engaging with affected stakeholders.
  - Identifying and assessing adverse impacts.
  - Taking actions to address adverse impacts.
  - Tracking effectiveness and communicating outcomes.
  - Elements are mapped to ESRS references.
- Risk management and internal controls [GOV-5]:
  - The Group operates an internal control system tailored to its business scale, ensuring operational effectiveness, reporting reliability, and compliance with laws, internal regulations, supervisory recommendations, and market standards.
  - Established external reporting process addresses non-compliance risks (deadlines, data quality, misclassification, missing disclosures).
  - Mitigations include partial automation, ongoing verification, audits, controls, and report authorization; overall risk level assessed as moderate.
  - Work is underway to incorporate sustainability reporting risk into this framework.
  - No dedicated integration of sustainability-reporting control findings into internal functions yet; 2025 internal audit plan excludes a sustainability reporting audit.
  - A strategic internal audit plan for 2026–2028 will be developed in 2025; inclusion of a sustainability reporting audit will depend on risk analysis.
  - Audit results are periodically reported to management and supervisory bodies, and to the PFSA for the Bank and Bank Hipoteczny.
- Double materiality assessment [IRO-1, IRO-2]:
  - First assessment conducted in 2024 in line with ESRS, with external consultancy support, at Group and subsidiary levels.
  - Scope covers own activities and exposures, emphasizing asset structure, sectoral credit exposure, and geographic distribution.
  - Broad stakeholder engagement via a survey (Aug 13–Sep 20, 2024) targeting 330,483 stakeholders, including subsidiaries’ representatives, employees, external stakeholders, and experts.
  - Developed an initial universe of 245 impacts, 165 risks, and 119 opportunities, assessed by cross-functional internal experts and external advisors.
  - Leads into the Impact Materiality section.

nodes.title: DOUBLE MATERIALITY ASSESSMENT METHODOLOGY AND PROCESS
nodes.heading: DOUBLE MATERIALITY AS SESSMENT METHODOLOGY AND PROCESS
nodes.start_phrase: In 2024, the Bank's Group conducted its first double materiality assessment aime d at identifying key issues related to impacts, risks, and opportunities related to sustainable development.
nodes.summary:
- Outlines the core elements of the Sustainability Statement’s due diligence chapter, aligned with ESRS references: embedding due diligence in governance/strategy/business model; engaging affected stakeholders; identifying and assessing adverse impacts; taking action to address them; and tracking effectiveness and communicating.
- Describes the Group’s internal control system and risk management for reporting: ensures operational effectiveness, reliable disclosures, and legal/regulatory compliance; identifies key non-compliance risks in external reporting (deadlines, data quality, misclassification, missing disclosures) and mitigation measures (partial automation, verification, audits, controls, authorizations). Overall reporting risk assessed as moderate.
- Notes ongoing work to incorporate sustainability reporting risk into reporting processes; no dedicated integration of sustainability reporting control findings yet; 2025 internal audit plan excludes sustainability reporting, with potential inclusion in the 2026–2028 plan based on risk assessment. Audit results are reported to governing bodies and, for the Bank and Bank Hipoteczny, to the PFSA.
- Presents the Group’s first double materiality assessment (2024), compliant with ESRS and supported by external experts, covering Group and subsidiaries, own activities and exposures (asset structure, sector credit exposure, geographic distribution).
- Details stakeholder engagement via a large survey (13 Aug–20 Sep 2024) sent to 330,483 stakeholders (subsidiary reps, employees, external stakeholders, experts) to validate key topics.
- Builds an initial universe of 245 impacts, 165 risks, and 119 opportunities; evaluations conducted by cross-functional internal experts with external support.
- Explains impact materiality methodology: assesses actual/potential, positive/negative impacts using scale, scope, reversibility (severity), and likelihood on a five-point scale; expert-defined thresholds determine materiality.
- Explains financial materiality for risks/opportunities: assessed by likelihood and potential financial consequences (using Group gross profit and gross carrying value); ESG risk treated as cross-cutting and not yet integrated into overall risk management; opportunity management tied to strategic objectives; uses historical data, forecasts, and expert judgment; high/very high ratings deemed material.
- Reports outcomes: selection of key issues across five topics (climate change, own employee resources, consumers and end-users, business conduct, and others); approvals on 24 Oct, 18 Nov, and 27 Nov 2024; results underpin sustainability disclosures (Tables 36–39).
- Summarizes environmental materiality results (Table 36): climate change mitigation and energy are material for impacts/risks/opportunities; climate change adaptation is material for impacts and opportunities (not risks); pollution (air/water/soil, substances, microplastics), water and marine resources, biodiversity and ecosystems, and circular economy topics are not material.

nodes.title: IMPACT MATERIALITY
nodes.heading: IMPACT MATERIALI TY
nodes.start_phrase: The process of double materiality assessment began with the creation of a list of impacts resulting from both the Bank's own activities and its value chain, which were evaluated using a dedicated tool to determine their actual, potential, positive, or negative nature .
nodes.summary:
- Focus: Description of PKO Bank Polski S.A. Group’s 2024 double materiality assessment methodology, governance, and outcomes, forming the basis for sustainability disclosures.
- Impact materiality: Identified impacts across own operations and value chain; assessed on a five-point scale using four parameters—scale, scope, reversibility (defining severity), and likelihood. Impacts above an expert-set cut-off were deemed material.
- Financial materiality: Assessed via likelihood and potential financial consequences, referencing the Group’s gross profit and gross carrying value; aligned post hoc with impact results; five-point scale applied.
- Risk/opportunity assessment: Tools for risks and opportunities slightly differ; ESG risk treated as cross-cutting (not a standalone risk type). The identification, evaluation, and management of IRO are not yet integrated into the Bank’s overall risk management process.
- Opportunities: Identified, evaluated, and managed primarily through the operationalization of strategic objectives.
- Evidence base: Historical data, market forecasts, and expert analyses underpin evaluations. Risks/opportunities rated high or very high were considered material.
- Outcome: 15 material issues identified (13 in impacts/opportunities and 6 in risks), grouped into five topics: climate change, own employee resources, consumers and end-users, business conduct, and others.
- Approvals and governance: Results validated internally (24 Oct 2024), by the Sustainable Development Committee (18 Nov 2024), and the Management Board (27 Nov 2024).
- Disclosure linkage: Results underpin Group sustainability disclosures (Tables 36–37), the list of ESRS disclosure requirements (Table 38), and other EU data points (Table 39).
- Table 36 highlights (Environment):
  - Material: Climate change mitigation (E1) — impacts, risks, opportunities; Climate change adaptation (E1) — impacts and opportunities (not risk); Energy (E1) — impacts, risks, opportunities.
  - Not material: Pollution (E2) across all subtopics; Water and marine resources (E3); Biodiversity and ecosystems (E4); Circular economy (E5).

nodes.title: FINANCIAL MATERIALITY
nodes.heading: FINANCIAL MATERIALITY
nodes.start_phrase: Due to the schedule of the double materiality assessment process, the evaluation of risks and opportunities began before the impact materiality assessment was completed.
nodes.summary:
- Scope and purpose: PKO Bank Polski S.A. Group’s 2024 double materiality assessment under ESRS to identify material impacts, risks, and opportunities across own operations and the value chain, informing sustainability disclosures.
- Methodology for impact materiality: identification of actual/potential, positive/negative impacts; assessment parameters include scale, scope, reversibility, and likelihood; five-point rating; expert-defined thresholds determine materiality.
- Financial materiality approach: assessed via likelihood and potential financial consequences relative to Group gross profit and gross carrying value; five-point scales; based on historical data, forecasts, and expert judgment; items rated high/very high deemed material.
- Risk and opportunity governance: ESG risk treated as cross-cutting (not standalone); IRO identification/evaluation/management not yet integrated into the overall risk framework; opportunities managed through strategic objective operationalization.
- Validation and disclosure: results endorsed internally (24 Oct 2024), by the Sustainable Development Committee (18 Nov 2024), and Management Board (27 Nov 2024); underpin sustainability report disclosures and data mapping to EU requirements (Tables 36–39).
- Material topics selected: 15 issues mapped to five themes—climate change, own workforce, consumers and end-users, business conduct, and “other” (e.g., infrastructure, state security). Environmental subtopics on pollution, water/marine resources, biodiversity, and circular economy were not deemed material.
- Climate change (E1): mitigation, adaptation, and energy are material (impacts/opportunities; risks material for mitigation and energy but not for adaptation). Key impact areas include financed emissions, financing in high-CO2 sectors and disaster-prone areas, and support for transition/adaptation. Risks span transition dynamics (carbon pricing/taxes, regulatory shifts, supply chain constraints, social acceptance) and governance gaps at clients. Opportunities include energy storage, green bonds, growing demand for emission-reduction finance, low-emission transport and charging infrastructure, energy-efficient real estate, and low-emission construction.
- Own workforce (S1): material impacts/opportunities in working conditions and equal treatment (health, safety, ergonomics, development, anti-harassment, data security); opportunities in pay benchmarking, social dialogue, collective bargaining, work–life balance, and training.
- Consumers and end-users (S4): material impacts/opportunities in information quality, personal safety, inclusion, privacy/cybersecurity, fair communication/advice; opportunities in stronger security standards, non-discrimination, and financing safety/health-related innovation.
- Business conduct (G1): material across corporate culture, whistleblower protection, corruption/bribery, and political engagement (as a risk). Emphasis on reputation, compliance, preventing abuses, AML/CFT effectiveness, and culture resilience; opportunities from embedding sustainability and robust whistleblower frameworks.
- Other material issues: development of industry and strategic infrastructure (energy, defense, raw materials) and product compliance; opportunity-only item on operating amid/post conflict; risk of environmental degradation from financed industrial activities; opportunities in post-conflict reconstruction and infrastructure build-out, and product certification programs.
- Climate assessment process (E1.IRO-1): identified 6 material impacts, 10 risks, 11 opportunities; considered short-, medium-, and long-term horizons; combined qualitative/quantitative analysis using sector (NACE) exposure and emissions; financial impacts tied to exposed assets and gross profit. Findings highlight high exposure to portfolio emissions and transition risk, moderate adaptation risk, and significant growth potential in supporting sustainable energy, low-emission technologies, and early-stage energy storage in Poland.

nodes.title: DESCRIPTION OF THE PROCESSES TO IDENTIFY AND ASSESS MATERIAL CLIMATE-RELATED IMPACTS, RISKS AND OPPORTUNITIES [E1.IRO-1]
nodes.heading: DESCRIPTION OF THE PR OCESSES TO IDENTIFY AND ASSESS MATERIAL CLIMATE -RELATED IMPACTS , RISKS AND OPPORTUNITIES [E1.IRO -1]
nodes.start_phrase: Materiality assessment identified 6 impacts, 10 risks, and 11 opportunities related to climate change.
nodes.summary:
- Scope and approach: The Group conducted a climate materiality assessment identifying 6 impacts, 10 risks, and 11 opportunities across the value chain (upstream and downstream), considering actual and potential effects over short (≤1 year), medium (≤5 years), and long (>5 years) terms. Impacts were evaluated by scale, scope, irreversibility, severity, probability, and potential financial benefits; risks/opportunities were assessed qualitatively and quantitatively, including financial exposure, gross profit impact, sectoral (NACE) specifics, and client emissions.
- Key findings: High importance of mitigating climate change due to significant portfolio emissions and transition exposure in financed sectors. Energy transition presents both material risks and sizable opportunities. Adaptation is important for impacts and opportunities; physical risks are generally moderate to low. Effective management is crucial for long-term financial stability.
- Growth and efficiency potential: Opportunities include revenue growth, cost reduction, and operational optimization through new technologies, resource efficiency, and entry into green markets.
- Identified climate opportunities (examples): 
  - Issuing green bonds to finance sustainable and low-emission investments and expand the green credit portfolio.
  - Financing low-emission transport and related infrastructure (e.g., EV charging).
  - Supporting energy-climate transition via financing low-emission technologies.
  - Financing low-emission construction in response to trends and regulations, including products that lower primary energy demand and costs.
  - Early-stage financing of energy storage solutions in Poland.
  - Leveraging pro-transition regulations to gain competitive advantage and enhance reputation through products enabling energy efficiency and low-emission choices.
- Own operations and emissions management: Group-wide GHG accounting across Scopes 1–3 per GHG Protocol; actions include renewable energy purchasing, PV installation, branch thermal modernisation, energy-efficient lighting, and lower-emission fleet renewal. Environmental standards are being unified across the Group. Supplier ESG assessments are in place, and for the first time, Scope 3 Category 1 (purchased goods/services) emissions for 2024 were calculated.
- Impact distribution: The Bank’s own operational climate impact is relatively low; the most significant impact resides downstream in Scope 3 Category 15 (investments/financed emissions).
- Physical risk analysis (Poland properties): Using KLIMADA 2.0 (IPCC RCP 8.5) for floods, inundations, and hurricanes across 2030, 2040, 2050:
  - Locations at risk: 2030—60 (Lower Silesia 21, Małopolska 11, Silesia 28); 2040—67 (21/11/35); 2050—89 (25/25/39).
  - Risk increases: +12% by 2040 vs 2030; +48% by 2050 vs 2030.
  - Actions will be planned to mitigate/avoid identified risks; time horizons align with property life cycles.
- Transition and reputational risks: Main internal transition-related concerns include potential lack of preparedness of certain locations for sudden physical events and reputational risk if the Bank’s own transformation lags its influence on clients. Transition risks at the organizational level are not deemed significant across time horizons.

nodes.title: DESCRIPTION OF THE PROCESSES TO IDENTIFY AND ASSESS MATERIAL CLIMATE-RELATED IMPACTS, RISKS AND OPPORTUNITIES [E1.IRO-1] - Introduction
nodes.source_title: DESCRIPTION OF THE PROCESSES TO IDENTIFY AND ASSESS MATERIAL CLIMATE-RELATED IMPACTS, RISKS AND OPPORTUNITIES [E1.IRO-1]
nodes.source_heading: DESCRIPTION OF THE PR OCESSES TO IDENTIFY AND ASSESS MATERIAL CLIMATE -RELATED IMPACTS , RISKS AND OPPORTUNITIES [E1.IRO -1]
nodes.heading: DESCRIPTION OF THE PR OCESSES TO IDENTIFY AND ASSESS MATERIAL CLIMATE -RELATED IMPACTS , RISKS AND OPPORTUNITIES [E1.IRO -1]
nodes.start_phrase: Materiality assessment identified 6 impacts, 10 risks, and 11 opportunities related to climate change.
nodes.summary: PKO Bank Polski S.A. Group’s materiality assessment (E1.IRO-1) identified 6 climate-related impacts, 10 risks, and 11 opportunities across its upstream and downstream value chain, covering actual and potential effects over short (≤1 year), medium (≤5 years), and long (>5 years) horizons. Impacts were evaluated by scale, scope, irreversibility, severity, and probability, alongside potential benefits (revenue growth, cost reduction, process optimization). The assessment combined qualitative and quantitative analyses, measuring financial effects via exposed assets relative to the balance sheet and impacts on gross profit, and incorporated client sector data (NACE) and financed clients’ emissions. Findings highlight high exposure to portfolio emissions and significant transition risks in energy‑intensive sectors, making risk/opportunity management critical to long‑term financial stability. Adaptation was deemed important for impacts and opportunities, with related risks moderate to low. Key opportunities include issuing green bonds; financing low‑emission transport (electromobility, charging infrastructure) and technologies; supporting low‑emission construction and rising client demand for related financial products; early entry into energy storage in Poland; and leveraging pro‑transition regulations to gain competitive advantage and support customers’ thermomodernization and low‑emission vehicle purchases.

nodes.title: OWN ACTIVITIES
nodes.heading: OWN ACTIVITIES
nodes.start_phrase: The Bank identifies emissions resulting from its own operations for the entire Group.
nodes.summary:
- The Group sees market-wide regulatory changes promoting low-emission products as an opportunity to finance the energy transition (e.g., thermomodernization, low-emission vehicles), gain competitive advantage, and strengthen reputation.
- Own-operations emissions are identified Group-wide under GHG Protocol Scopes 1–3; reduction actions include renewable energy procurement, photovoltaic installations, branch thermal upgrades, energy‑efficient lighting, and gradual fleet replacement.
- Environmental protection rules are being standardized across the Group; an ESG-based supplier survey is in place, and for the first time Scope 3 Category 1 (purchased goods/services) emissions for suppliers were calculated for 2024.
- The Bank’s own operational climate impact is assessed as relatively low; the most significant impact lies downstream in Scope 3 Category 15 (investments), discussed elsewhere in the report.
- Physical climate risk analysis for properties in Poland used KLIMADA 2.0 (IPCC RCP 8.5) across three horizons (to 2030, 2040, 2050), focusing on floods, inundations, and hurricanes; exposure threshold set at ≥0.75 at municipality level.
- Physical risks affect units in Lower Silesia, Małopolska, and Silesia, with risk locations rising from 60 (2030) to 67 (2040, +12%) and 89 (2050, +48% vs. 2030); risk‑mitigation actions will be planned and implemented.
- Transition-related events for own operations and supply chain include possible site preparedness gaps for sudden risks and reputational risk if the Bank’s own transformation lags customers’; overall transition risks are not significant at the organizational level across time horizons.
- No cases of locked-in emissions or taxonomy compliance failures were identified.
- Scenario assumptions align with those used for Scope 3 Categories 13 and 15 (credit portfolio).
- Portfolio climate risk analysis quantitatively covers PKO Bank Polski, PKO Bank Hipoteczny, PKO Leasing, PKO Faktoring, PCM, and KREDOBANK (the latter for transition risk only); other subsidiaries underwent qualitative assessment under double materiality.
- Physical risk exposure in lending portfolios uses KLIMADA 2.0 data for drought/water scarcity, floods/inundations, and hurricanes across 2030/2040/2050, linked to default likelihood; results feed into capital adequacy disclosures and climate stress tests (E1.SBM-3).
- Insurance portfolios (PKO TU and PKO Życie) consider an extended set of physical risks (e.g., multiple flood types, heavy precipitation, drought, heatwaves) and long-term changes in temperature/precipitation; expected effects include higher property claims and potential large/cumulative losses (assessed low materiality), increased life claims from harsher conditions, and climate-driven macro effects raising claims in financial, motor, and health lines (low materiality). PFSA stress test scenarios are integrated into risk management and planning (SBM-3).
- Transition risk exposure is assessed via lending to non-financial sectors with significant climate impact (NACE A, B, C, D, E, F, G, H, I, L) and entities meeting EU 2020/1818 Art. 12(1)(d–g) criteria; identification uses expert review, classifying fossil fuel, oil/gas, and electricity producers, with a conservative assumption that non‑RES electricity producers earn ≥50% of revenue from electricity generation. Scenario analysis for transition risks is detailed in climate stress tests (E1.SBM-3).

nodes.title: PORTFOLIO ANALYSIS
nodes.heading: PORTFOLIO ANALYSIS
nodes.start_phrase: The impact of different types of climate risk is quantitatively analysed in relation to the portfolios of PKO Bank Polski, PKO Bank Hipoteczny, PKO Leasing, PKO Faktoring, PCM, and KREDOBANK (the KREDOBANK portfolio is analysed solely with respect to exposure to transition risk).
nodes.summary:
- Confirms no locked-in greenhouse gas emissions or taxonomy compliance breaches; identifies operational areas exposed to physical climate risks and outlines preparation actions.
- Describes climate scenario alignment with prior scope 3 (categories 13 and 15) analyses for the credit portfolio.
- Portfolio analysis:
  - Quantitative climate risk assessment for PKO Bank Polski, PKO Bank Hipoteczny, PKO Leasing, PKO Faktoring, PCM, and KREDOBANK (transition risk only); qualitative assessment for other subsidiaries via double materiality.
  - Physical risk methodology uses KLIMADA 2.0 (IPCC RCP 8.5) by client/collateral location, covering drought/water scarcity, flooding/inundations, and hurricanes across 2030, 2040, 2050; exposure linked to probability of default; integrated into climate stress tests.
  - References detailed results in the “Capital Adequacy and Other Information…” report (Form 5) and in E1.SBM-3.
- Insurance portfolios (PKO TU and PKO Życie):
  - Considers acute risks (various flood types, heavy precipitation, drought, heatwaves) and chronic risks (precipitation/temperature changes).
  - Qualitative assessment anticipates more claims and potential cumulative damages in property insurance (low materiality) and increased life insurance claims due to harsher conditions; notes inflation/unemployment/market instability may raise damages in financial, motor, and health insurance (low materiality).
  - Incorporates PFSA-developed stress test scenarios into ongoing risk management, planning, and strategy.
- Transition risk assessment:
  - Measures exposure to non-financial companies with significant climate impact (NACE A, B, C, D, E, F, G, H, I, L) and to entities per Article 12(1)(d–g) of Delegated Regulation (EU) 2020/1818.
  - Uses expert portfolio reviews to identify fossil fuel, oil, gas, and electricity producers; conservatively classifies non-RES electricity producers as deriving ≥50% of revenue from electricity.
  - Scenario analysis for transition risks is addressed through climate stress tests (E1.SBM-3).
- ESRS reporting coverage (Table 38):
  - Maps where the report covers ESRS 2 (general disclosures), ESRS E1 (climate change), ESRS S1 (own workforce), ESRS S4 (consumers/end-users), and ESRS G1 (business conduct), with chapter references (13.1, 13.2.2, 13.3.1, 13.3.2, 13.4).
- Alignment with other EU legislation and disclosure status (Table 39):
  - Cross-references ESRS datapoints to SFDR, CRR Pillar 3, Benchmark Regulation, and EU Climate Law, indicating where disclosures are made in the sustainability statement.
  - Notes application of a transition period with no 2024 disclosure for certain ESRS E1-9 physical and opportunity-related metrics.
  - Identifies items not applicable (e.g., E1-5 fossil energy details for high-impact sectors, E1-7 carbon credits) and topics considered not relevant to the Group (e.g., E2 pollutants, E3 water/marine, E4 biodiversity/land/deforestation, E5 waste, S2 value-chain workers, S3 affected communities).
- Stakeholder engagement for double materiality (SBM-2):
  - Conducted online surveys (Microsoft Forms) and internal tools engaging subsidiaries, employees, institutional investors, customers, business partners, auditors, media, the public, and NGOs.
  - Input focused on the 2025–2027 Strategy pillars, including energy transition financing and customer accessibility, and informed topic completeness and the Group’s influence assessment.

nodes.title: INTERESTS AND VIEWS OF STAKEHOLDERS [SBM-2]
nodes.heading: INTERESTS AND VIEWS O F STAKEHOLDERS [SBM-2]
nodes.start_phrase: To ensure a broad spectrum of impacts, risks, and opportunities related to the activities of the Bank’s Group were considered, stakeholders were involved in the double materiality assessment.
nodes.summary:
- ESRS coverage and materiality:
  - Several social topics were assessed as not material for the Group, including: ESRS S2 (value chain workers) policies, non-respect of UNGPs/OECD guidelines, ILO Convention due diligence, and value-chain human rights incidents; and ESRS S3 (affected communities) human rights policy commitments, non-respect of UNGPs/ILO/OECD, and human rights incidents.
  - ESRS S4 (consumers and end-users) disclosures are addressed (policies, UNGPs/OECD alignment, human rights issues) with cross-references to section 13.3.2.
  - ESRS G1 (business conduct) disclosures cover adherence to the UN Convention against Corruption, whistle-blower protection, standards on anti-corruption/anti-bribery, and reporting of fines (section 13.4).
  - References to EU regulatory frameworks include Delegated Regulations 2020/1816 and 2020/1818, SFDR, CRR, the Benchmarks Regulation, and the European Climate Law.

- Stakeholder engagement and double materiality [SBM-2]:
  - A double materiality assessment was conducted with internal and external stakeholders via surveys (Microsoft Forms for externals and internal tools), involving subsidiaries, investors, customers, partners, auditors, media, the public, NGOs, and employees.
  - Results confirmed completeness of topics; no strategy or business model changes were required. Outcomes were presented to the Sustainable Development Committee (18 Nov 2024) and approved by the Management Board (26 Nov 2024).
  - Twelve significant stakeholder groups were identified with mapped influence and engagement methods: employees; shareholders/investors; clients; business partners; regulators/supervisors; rating agencies; auditors; media/public opinion; local communities; the natural environment; competition; and employees in the value chain.

- Key stakeholder expectations and the Bank’s responses:
  - Clients: demand innovative, secure, accessible digital services and products supporting sustainability (clean energy, low-emission transport, building modernization). The Bank expands mobile/online services and green products.
  - Employees: seek stability, development, and a diverse, inclusive culture; the Bank provides training, promotes culture and diversity, and monitors satisfaction (eNPS).
  - Shareholders: expect profitability, transparency, and ESG integration; addressed through strategy and ESG reporting.
  - Regulators: require compliance with financial and environmental rules; integrated into policies, disclosures, credit, and procurement.
  - Local communities: value financial education and regional development; supported via programs and sponsorships.
  - The Bank integrates ESG criteria into product design, credit and procurement processes, risk assessment, and actively finances Poland’s green transition (renewables, low-emission vehicles, thermal modernization, green bonds, SME ESG loans), aiming to increase the share of ESG-aligned loans.

- Future commitments and strategic direction:
  - Net-zero by 2050: reduce own emissions (over 90% green energy use, lower building energy intensity) and decarbonize the loan portfolio via sectoral pathways.
  - By 2027: target a 20% share in bank financing for Poland’s energy transition by growing green energy lending.
  - Enhance ESG reporting and stakeholder communication; develop AI and blockchain-based platforms to improve service and security; continue social initiatives (financial education, future skills, environmental actions).

- Anticipated stakeholder impacts:
  - Customers: stronger loyalty and perception of PKO as a green finance leader.
  - Employees: higher satisfaction and engagement through development and diversity initiatives.
  - Shareholders: potential valuation uplift and lower funding costs from innovation and responsible performance.
  - Local communities: strengthened relationships and reputation through ongoing social activities.

- Material impacts, risks, opportunities, and linkage to strategy [SBM-3]:
  - The double materiality process identified environmental and social impacts with defined time horizons (short <1 year, medium, long >5 years), to be reviewed in the next cycle.
  - These topics are embedded in the PKO Bank Polski Strategy 2025–2027 and the business model, supporting sustainable growth and the resilience of the Polish economy.

nodes.title: MATERIAL IMPACTS, RISKS AND OPPORTUNITIES AND THEIR INTERACTION WITH STRATEGY AND BUSINESS MODEL [SBM-3]
nodes.heading: MATERIAL IMPACTS , RISKS AND OPPORTUNI TIES AND THEIR INTER ACTION WITH STRATEGY AND BUSINESS MODEL [SBM-3]
nodes.start_phrase: As part of the double materiality assessmen t, areas of impact of the Bank’s Group on people and the environment were identified, which are presented in Table 41.
nodes.summary:
- Stakeholder-driven ESG approach: enhanced transparency and reporting; expansion of sustainable products and community support; growth of secure, accessible digital services; financial education initiatives.
- Future model and targets: net-zero by 2050 via own-emission cuts and portfolio decarbonization; by 2027, 20% share in financing Poland’s energy transition; stronger ESG reporting and stakeholder communication; development of AI/blockchain banking platforms; continued social and educational programs.
- Stakeholder impacts: improved customer experience and green finance positioning; higher employee satisfaction via development, diversity, and better conditions; stronger shareholder trust and valuation from innovation and responsibility; strengthened ties with local communities.
- Double materiality assessment: identification of material positive and negative impacts across ESRS E1 (climate), S1 (workforce), S4 (consumers), G1 (business conduct), and specific topics (industrial development, product compliance, post-war reconstruction), with time horizons and value-chain mapping.
- Key impacts highlighted: financed emissions and high-CO2 projects; exposure to disaster-prone areas; green leasing/fleet modernization; transition costs vs long-term emission reductions; workforce health, ergonomics, training, and risks (harassment, data loss, human rights); consumer privacy, fair communication, advice quality; business conduct issues (reputation, advertising/sponsorship governance, foundation documentation, anti-corruption, whistleblowing); infrastructure investment benefits; energy security; product compliance driving loyalty.
- Strategy-business model link: focus on low-emission financing, disaster-risk-aware project selection, ethical conduct and transparency, cost-efficient marketing/sponsorship, emissions-compliant leasing, employee well-being and communication, robust data/cybersecurity, adherence to international anti-corruption standards, and active financing of infrastructure/RES; ESG-aligned product development.
- Material risks: transition/energy risks (investment costs, project delays, EUA price spikes, supply bottlenecks, social acceptance issues); regulatory shocks (carbon taxes, building energy rules); lack of decarbonization strategies; political engagement backlash; weak corporate culture; AML/CFT failures; environmental degradation from financed industry.
- Material opportunities: financing RES, storage, EV charging, low-emission transport; issuing/investing in green bonds; energy-efficient real estate and sustainable construction; workforce policies (pay, social dialogue, collective bargaining, work-life balance, training) boosting productivity and employer brand; stronger consumer trust via transparency, privacy, and cybersecurity; inclusive finance; ethical culture and whistleblower protections; post-war reconstruction; large-scale energy/transport infrastructure; product compliance and certifications.
- Financial effects: near-term higher operational/ESG compliance costs, increased credit provisions, collateral value declines, liquidity pressures from climate risks, project and reputational risks; offset by revenue growth from green products, energy-efficient mortgages, enhanced reputation, and customer loyalty through digital security and transparency.
- Outlook: short term—higher costs and new green-product revenues; medium term—cost optimization, stronger stability and revenues from sustainable sectors; long term—greater portfolio profitability, asset growth in energy transition, and market leadership in sustainability.
- Strategic context and KPIs (2025–2027): universal bank across Poland and selected European markets; 25,884 employees; PLN 41,451m revenues in 2024; no operations in fossil fuels; by 2027—20% energy transition financing share, >50% loan portfolio with decarbonization plans, gender pay gap <5%, >33% underrepresented gender in governing bodies and >40% in senior management, >70% suppliers adhering to Code of Ethics, >90% employees ESG-trained; net-zero by 2050.
- Sustainable finance offering: sustainability-linked and green bonds; green and sustainability-linked loans; energy-efficient residential and commercial mortgages aligned with EP/CBI criteria; renovation loans with BGK bonuses; RES financing (including PV) via loans/leasing; eco-loans; BGK guarantees (BIZNESMAX PLUS, EKOMAX); FENG eco-loan.

nodes.title: IMPACT OF THE STRATEGY ON SUSTAINABLE DEVELOPMENT [SBM-1]
nodes.heading: IMPACT OF THE STRATE GY ON SUSTAINABLE DE VELOPMENT [SBM-1]
nodes.start_phrase: PKO Bank Polski S.A. is a universal bank that operates in both the retail segment (individuals, businesses, and enterprises) and the corporate and investment segment (corporations, government and local government entities, and foreign customers).
nodes.summary:
- Context and scope: PKO Bank Polski S.A. Group Director’s Report for 2024 highlights operations across Poland and in Germany, the Czech Republic, Slovakia, Ukraine, Sweden, and Ireland; 25,884 employees as of 31 Dec 2024; PLN 41,451 million in revenues; no entities active in fossil fuel or high climate‑impact sectors.
- Key risk themes: rising regulatory costs with readiness to adapt (including CO2 reduction in own operations and loan portfolio); structured reputation management with transparency and social impact focus; mitigation of project delay risk through developing technical expertise in financed technologies.
- ESG strategy 2025–2027: targets to strengthen market position with KPIs by 2027—20% share in financing Poland’s energy transition; >50% of loan portfolio covered by decarbonisation plans; gender pay gap <5%; >33% underrepresented gender in governance bodies; >40% underrepresented gender in senior management (B‑1, B‑2); >70% supplier/partner adherence to the Code of Ethics; >90% employee ESG training completion. Long‑term goal: net‑zero GHG emissions by 2050.
- Sustainable finance offering: broad suite including sustainability‑linked bonds and loans; green bonds; green/energy‑efficient mortgages; loans for energy‑efficient commercial buildings; renovation/thermal modernization loans with BGK bonuses; green/RES investment loans; BGK guarantees (BIZNESMAX PLUS, BIZNESMAX, EKOMAX); PKO eco‑loan; FENG eco‑loan with ecological premium; financing/leasing for PV equipment, wind turbines, heat pumps; EV leasing under the “Mój elektryk” program with BOŚ; financing for EV charging points and high‑power stations with storage; loans for PV farms; InvestEU‑backed leasing/loans for RES for SMEs and mid‑caps.
- Emissions and client engagement: energy‑sector corporate clients and mortgage borrowers are key emission drivers; relationship management and promotion of low‑emission solutions are central to portfolio decarbonisation.
- Value chain overview (SBM‑1): 
  - Activities: internal economy (HR, operations, innovation), supply/distribution (supplier cooperation, marketing, branches, digital channels), and external environment (geographical, regulatory, financial; monitoring trends and geopolitical/regulatory risks).
  - Resources: human capital; branch and IT infrastructure; relationships with customers (service/loyalty/feedback), suppliers (long‑term, tech access), partners (financial/tech innovation), and regulators (transparent, compliant).
  - Segments: upstream (energy; IT equipment and licenses; IT services incl. cloud, mobile/insurance apps); own operations (banking, insurance, leasing, factoring, investment funds); downstream (key clients by turnover/sectors; agents and intermediaries).
- Market conduct: the Group does not identify banned products or services in specific markets.

nodes.title: VALUE CHAIN [SBM-1]
nodes.heading: VALUE CHAIN [SBM -1]
nodes.start_phrase: The value chain of the Bank's Group is a complex system of activities, resources, and relationships used in business operations, from the concept stage to the delivery, consumption, and withdrawal of products or services from the market.
nodes.summary:
- Green financing offer: EV leasing via the “Mój Elektryk” program; financing for wind turbines, heat pumps, and other prosumer RES; financing/leasing for EV charging points and high-power charging stations with storage; loans for photovoltaic farms; RES financing with InvestEU guarantees for SMEs.
- No identification of banned products/services in specific markets.
- Emissions focus: energy-sector corporate clients and retail mortgage clients are key to financed emissions; relationship management and promotion of low-emission transitions are central to decarbonization.
- Value chain overview: internal operations, supply/distribution channels, and external environment monitoring (market, regulatory, geopolitical risks).
- Key resources and relationships: human capital; branch and IT infrastructure; customer, supplier, partner (financial/tech), and regulator relations to drive innovation and compliance.
- Upstream suppliers: energy; IT equipment and software licenses; cloud/mobile/insurance IT services; vehicle fleet; cash handling equipment; Visa/Mastercard; office equipment; mostly Polish suppliers with some EU sourcing.
- Procurement: >6,000 suppliers registered; 389 procedures in 2024 resulting in 516 contracts; focus categories include software, materials/equipment, administrative services, IT security, and non-IT consulting; predominantly long-term contracts with Polish firms; outsourcing list published.
- Own operations: banking, insurance, leasing, factoring, investment funds, and other services (incl. property management); footprint in Poland, Ukraine, Sweden, Ireland, Czech Republic, Germany, Slovakia, Romania.
- Customer base: 12.1 million retail customers; 32.7 thousand corporate/municipal/financial institution customers.
- Downstream/distribution: agents and intermediaries; 203 agents operating 249 agencies; 64 mortgage intermediaries; investments for private/business clients; waste and end-of-life product handling.
- Business model: universal bank, largest in Poland by assets, equity, loans, deposits, network, customers, and employees; provides services via branches, agencies, and digital channels; extensive subsidiary offerings (mortgages, leasing, factoring, funds, pensions, insurance, fleet, transfer agent, tech, real estate); banking and financial services also in Ukraine.
- Financials and impact: income from interest, fees/commissions, and other sources; profits distributed per supervisory allowances; supports the economy, environment, and local communities.
- Strategy and data: uses comprehensive market/economic analysis including energy transition trends; plans to expand sustainability data coverage and analytics capabilities.
- Sustainable finance products: SLLs for corporates with pricing linked to sustainability KPIs (e.g., emissions); retail eco-loans with rate reductions tied to low-emission uses (e.g., RES); benefits include reduced financed GHG emissions and improved environmental outcomes for the Bank and its clients.

nodes.title: BUSINESS MODEL [SBM-1]
nodes.heading: BUSINESS MODEL [SBM -1]
nodes.start_phrase: The Bank’s Group is a leading financial institution in Central and Eastern Europe.
nodes.summary:
- Scope and context: Excerpt from PKO Bank Polski S.A. Group Director’s Report 2024 covering value chain, procurement, geographic footprint, customer reach, distribution model, business model, sustainability strategy, and EU Taxonomy disclosures.

- Value chain and procurement:
  - Suppliers predominantly based in Poland, with some EU sourcing due to varied business models.
  - Key procurement categories: software, IT security, consulting (non-IT), materials/equipment, and administrative services; typical purchases include vehicle fleet, cash handling equipment, payment network services (Visa/Mastercard), and office equipment.
  - Supplier base exceeds 6,000; in 2024, 389 procurement procedures led to 516 (mostly long-term) contracts; nearly all suppliers are Polish.
  - The Bank publishes a list of outsourced service providers on its website.

- Geographic presence and customers:
  - Operations in Poland, Ukraine, Sweden, Ireland, Czech Republic, Germany, Slovakia, and Romania.
  - Customer base: 12.1 million retail clients and 32.7 thousand corporate/municipal/financial institution clients.

- Distribution channels:
  - Agency network: 203 agents operating 249 agencies.
  - Housing loans also distributed via 64 mortgage intermediaries.

- Business model (SBM-1):
  - PKO Bank Polski is the largest commercial bank in Poland and a leading CEE financial institution by assets, equity, loans, deposits, distribution network, customers, and employees.
  - Universal banking services offered through branches, agencies, and digital channels, with emphasis on customer education.
  - Group subsidiaries provide mortgage lending, leasing, factoring, investment and pension funds, insurance, fleet management, transfer agency, technology solutions, real estate management; operates banking and debt collection in Ukraine.
  - Revenue from interest, fees/commissions, and other sources; profits distributed subject to supervisory permissions; supports the economy, environment, and local communities.

- Strategy and sustainability:
  - Strategy grounded in economic/market analyses and financial planning, with expanded data on energy transition, low-emission economy, customer needs, market dynamics, and competitive positioning.
  - Sustainable finance offerings:
    - Sustainability-linked loans (SLLs) for corporates with interest rates tied to ESG KPIs (e.g., emissions reduction).
    - Eco-loans for retail clients with favorable rates for financing low-emission technologies (e.g., renewables).
  - Benefits include reduced financed GHG emissions, lower transition risk for shareholders, and heightened internal focus on sustainability.
  - Ongoing development of ESG data collection and reporting; select metrics disclosed in periodic and capital adequacy reports.

- Environmental information and EU Taxonomy (Article 8) disclosures:
  - Disclosures prepared under Regulation (EU) 2020/852 and applicable delegated regulations (2021/2139, 2021/2178, 2022/1214, 2023/2485, 2023/2486, 2024/3215).
  - EU Taxonomy described as the classification system for environmentally sustainable activities to enhance market transparency and comparability and support investor decisions.

- Stakeholder benefits highlighted: for shareholders, reduced transition risk in moving to a low‑emission economy; for employees, explicit integration of sustainability considerations in operations.
- Reporting practices include periodic disclosure of sustainable financing volumes and reductions in financed emissions intensity, including in the capital adequacy report.
- Ongoing enhancement of ESG data collection systems to better measure sustainability impacts.
- Environmental Information section (13.2.1) details disclosures under Article 8 of the EU Taxonomy Regulation (EU) 2020/852.
- Comprehensive legal basis cited: core Taxonomy Regulation and multiple Commission Delegated Regulations (2021/2139, 2021/2178, 2022/1214, 2023/2485, 2023/2486, 2024/3215) defining technical screening criteria, disclosure content/presentation, sectoral additions, and corrections.
- Clarifies the purpose of the EU Taxonomy as a classification system to enhance market transparency and comparability and to support investor decision-making regarding environmentally sustainable activities.
