nodes.heading: 13.2.1 DISCLOSURES PURSUANT TO ARTICLE 8 OF REGULATION (EU) 2020/852 (TAXONOMY REGULATION )
nodes.start_phrase: The taxonomy disclosure of the PKO Bank Polski S.A. Group has been prepared on the basis of a package of regulations that have been implemented into European law by Regulation (EU) 2020/ 852 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 18 June 2020 on the establishment of a framework to facilitate sustainable investment, and amending Regulation (EU) 2019/2088 (hereinafter: EU Taxonomy or Regulation (EU) 2020/852) together with the following delegated regulations:
nodes.summary:
- Emphasizes the Bank’s integration of sustainability into operations, highlighting benefits for shareholders (reduced transition risk) and employees (clear prioritization of sustainability).
- Notes reporting of key ESG metrics—such as financing that supports sustainable development and the intensity of financed emissions—in periodic reports, including the capital adequacy report.
- States ongoing development of systems to collect and improve ESG data measurement across the Group.
- Introduces Section 13.2 “Environmental Information” and the Article 8 EU Taxonomy disclosure requirements.
- Defines the legal basis and scope of the Group’s Taxonomy disclosures, citing Regulation (EU) 2020/852 and a suite of delegated regulations (2021/2139, 2021/2178, 2022/1214, 2023/2485, 2023/2486, 2024/3215).
- Summarizes what these delegated acts cover: technical screening criteria for climate change mitigation and adaptation; criteria for other environmental objectives (water/marine resources, circular economy, pollution prevention, biodiversity); disclosure content and presentation; sector-specific disclosures; and textual corrections.
- Concludes with a brief explanation of the EU Taxonomy’s purpose as a classification system to enhance market transparency, comparability, and support investor decision-making regarding sustainable activities.

nodes.title: GENERAL INFORMATION - LEGAL BASIS AND SCOPE OF DISCLOSURE
nodes.heading: GENERAL INFORMATION - LEGAL BASIS AND SCO PE OF DISCLOSURE
nodes.start_phrase: The taxonomy disclosure of the PKO Bank Polski S.A. Group has been prepared on the basis of a package of regulations that have been implemented into European law by Regulation (EU) 2020/ 852 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 18 June 2020 on the establishment of a framework to facilitate sustainable investment, and amending Regulation (EU) 2019/2088 (hereinafter: EU Taxonomy or Regulation (EU) 2020/852) together with the following delegated regulations:
nodes.summary:
- The report outlines PKO Bank Polski Group’s approach to sustainability, noting benefits for shareholders (reduced transition risk) and employees, and ongoing upgrades to ESG data systems with select metrics reported periodically (e.g., capital adequacy report).
- It presents Environmental Information with disclosures under Article 8 of the EU Taxonomy Regulation (EU) 2020/852, detailing the legal basis and a comprehensive list of relevant delegated regulations (2021–2024) governing technical screening criteria and disclosure requirements.
- The document explains the EU Taxonomy’s purpose as a classification system for environmentally sustainable activities and sets out the four conditions for taxonomy alignment (substantial contribution, DNSH, minimum safeguards, and technical screening criteria).
- It lists the six environmental objectives covered: climate change mitigation and adaptation, sustainable use and protection of water and marine resources, circular economy, pollution prevention and control, and biodiversity and ecosystems.
- Scope: a full 2024 taxonomy analysis at transaction level across all six objectives (with specific focus on CCM and CCA), broken down by customer segment, financial instrument, and activity type, with results presented in KPI templates.
- It notes separate disclosure on exposures related to nuclear and natural gas activities.
- Key Performance Indicators: compliance with Article 8 requires a consolidated sustainability statement, with the primary KPI being the Green Asset Ratio (GAR).
- GAR is defined as the share of assets financing taxonomy-aligned activities within core lending and investment (loans, advances, debt securities, equity) and is calculated on a prudential consolidation basis using FINREP; entities in scope are listed in the Group’s capital adequacy report.
- The GAR numerator includes non-trading book exposures to: (1) financial enterprises, (2) non-financial enterprises meeting defined reporting criteria, and (3) households for residential property, building renovation, and motor vehicle loans.

nodes.title: SCOPE OF TAXONOMY DISCLOSURE
nodes.heading: SCOPE OF TAXONOMY DIS CLOSURE
nodes.start_phrase: The Bank’s Group's disclosure for 2024 provides a full taxonomic analysis of the Bank’s Group's individual transactions in terms of both eligibility for the taxonomy and compliance with the taxonomy in relation to the six environmental objectives, as well as the first two objectives: climate change mitigation (CCM) and climate change adaptation (CCA).
nodes.summary:
- Outlines the EU Taxonomy framework, specifying four conditions for an activity to be environmentally sustainable: substantial contribution to objectives, do-no-significant-harm (DNSH), compliance with minimum safeguards, and meeting technical screening criteria set by EU delegated acts.
- Lists the six environmental objectives: climate change mitigation, climate change adaptation, sustainable use and protection of water and marine resources, transition to a circular economy, pollution prevention and control, and protection and restoration of biodiversity and ecosystems.
- Explains that technical screening criteria define when an activity significantly contributes to an objective without harming others.
- Describes the 2024 scope of PKO Bank Polski S.A. Group’s taxonomy disclosure: full transaction-level analysis of eligibility and alignment across all six objectives, with focused reporting on climate change mitigation and adaptation; results are segmented by customer segment, financial instrument, and activity and presented in KPI tables; separate disclosure of exposures to nuclear and natural gas activities.
- Details Key Performance Indicators (Templates 0–5), centered on the Green Asset Ratio (GAR) required under Article 8 of the EU Taxonomy and Directive 2013/34/EU, indicating the share of assets financing taxonomy-aligned activities across loans, advances, debt securities, and equity instruments.
- States that GAR is calculated on a prudential consolidation basis using FINREP data, with entities covered listed in the Group’s capital adequacy disclosure.
- Specifies assets included in the GAR numerator: non-trading book exposures to qualifying financial and non-financial enterprises (per Articles 19a/29a of Directive 2013/34/EU) and household exposures for residential property, building renovation, and motor vehicle loans.

nodes.summary:
- Explains the EU Taxonomy framework, detailing the four conditions for an activity to be environmentally sustainable (substantial contribution, DNSH, minimum safeguards, technical screening criteria) and lists the six environmental objectives (CCM, CCA, WTR, CE, PPC, BIO), emphasizing the role of technical screening criteria.
- Defines the scope of PKO Bank Polski S.A. Group’s 2024 taxonomy disclosure: a full analysis of individual transactions for eligibility and alignment, broken down by customer segment, financial instrument, and activity; includes dedicated disclosure on exposures to nuclear and natural gas.
- Describes the required Key Performance Indicators (KPIs) under Article 8 of the EU Taxonomy, with the Green Asset Ratio (GAR) as the main KPI for credit institutions, showing the share of assets financing taxonomy-aligned activities within total qualifying assets.
- Details the GAR calculation approach: based on prudential consolidation and FINREP; numerator includes non-trading book exposures (loans, advances, debt securities, equity) to qualifying financial and non-financial enterprises, households (residential property, renovation, motor vehicle loans), local authorities (housing/specialist funding), and repossessed real estate; denominator includes all on-balance-sheet assets excluding exposures to central governments, central banks, supranational issuers, and the trading book.
- Outlines reporting templates used (Annex VI to Delegated Regulation (EU) 2021/2178): 
  - Template 0 (summary of KPIs), 
  - Template 1 (on- and off-balance-sheet assets in GAR), 
  - Template 2 (exposures to non-financial enterprises by NACE-4 sectors), 
  - Template 3 (GAR stock), 
  - Template 4 (new 2024 flows), 
  - Template 5 (off-balance-sheet KPIs for guarantees and assets under management), 
  - plus a table with weighted averages for mixed-group taxonomy-aligned activities.
- Notes GAR is disclosed using two lenses: Turnover KPI and CapEx KPI, and includes prior-year (T-1) comparatives.
- Presents key 2024 results (Template 0):
  - GAR stock: PLN 6,821.11m environmentally sustainable assets (by CapEx); 1.86% (Turnover KPI) and 1.96% (CapEx KPI); 65.95% coverage over total assets; 40.01% of assets excluded from GAR numerator; 34.05% excluded from GAR denominator.
  - GAR flow (new 2024 exposures): PLN 1,895.82m; 2.60% (Turnover KPI) and 2.70% (CapEx KPI); 50.49% coverage; 33.32% of assets excluded from numerator; 49.51% excluded from denominator.
  - Off-balance sheet: financial guarantees reported as 0; assets under management: PLN 1,048.54m with 2.03% (Turnover KPI) and 4.81% (CapEx KPI).

nodes.summary: Introduces PKO Bank Polski Group’s EU Taxonomy KPI disclosures (Templates 0–5) for 31 December 2024 under Article 8, centering on the Green Asset Ratio (GAR) calculated on a prudential consolidation basis (Regulation (EU) 575/2013) using FINREP. Defines GAR numerator exposures as non-trading book loans, advances, debt securities and equities to qualifying financial and non-financial enterprises (Directive 2013/34/EU Arts. 19a/29a), households (residential property, building renovation, motor vehicles), local authorities (housing/specialist funding), and repossessed real estate; the denominator includes all on-balance-sheet assets excluding exposures to central governments, central banks, supranational issuers, and the trading book. Disclosures cover taxonomy alignment for climate change mitigation and adaptation and eligibility across all six environmental objectives, with breakdowns by customer segment and instrument. Describes Template 0 (summary KPIs), Template 1 (on/off-balance-sheet assets in GAR), Template 2 (non-financial enterprise exposures with NACE-4 mapping), Template 3 (GAR on stock), Template 4 (2024 flow for new exposures), Template 5 (off-balance-sheet KPIs for financial guarantees and assets under management), and Table 61 (weighted average KPIs for the mixed group). GAR is reported using both Turnover KPI and CapEx KPI of counterparties’ taxonomy-eligible/aligned activities per Annex VI of Delegated Regulation (EU) 2021/2178. Notes this is the Group’s second taxonomy disclosure with 2023 (T‑1) comparatives and references the prudential consolidation entity list in the 31 Dec 2024 capital adequacy report.

nodes.summary:
- Purpose and scope: Excerpt from PKO Bank Polski S.A. Group’s 2024 Director’s Report detailing EU Taxonomy disclosures, key performance indicators (KPIs), data sources, and minimum safeguards assessment within a prudential consolidation scope.
- Segments and consolidation: The Group operates in banking (including leasing and factoring, treated akin to lending) and asset management; it is not a financial conglomerate. Taxonomy disclosures are prepared on a prudentially consolidated basis within a consolidated sustainability report.
- KPI methodology: In line with Commission Notice (EU) C/2024/6691, the Group calculates a consolidated taxonomy KPI and, for prudentially consolidated subsidiaries, KPI Turnover and KPI CapEx as weighted averages across segments. Weights reflect each segment’s share of total consolidated revenue.
- Entities in scope (Directive 2013/34/EU): Identification focuses on customers obliged to disclose sustainability information, namely:
  - Large public-interest entities with >500 employees.
  - Public-interest parent companies of large groups with >500 employees on a consolidated basis and their consolidated subsidiaries.
- Data sources and verification:
  - Primary sources: Companies’ latest non-financial reports, Notoria ESG Module (including indicators such as OECD principles violations), and EMIS for group structures and subsidiary listings.
  - Process: Compile financed subsidiaries consolidated by parent companies using internal systems and EMIS; cross-check disclosures with Notoria and company reports.
- Minimum safeguards assessment (EU Taxonomy Article 18):
  - Method: Analyze Notoria ESG data and company non-financial reports; apply expert judgment to assign YES/NO on safeguards compliance.
  - Reporting treatment: Entities not meeting minimum safeguards are classified as taxonomy-eligible but not taxonomy-aligned.
  - Group-wide assumption: If a parent company confirms compliance, all its consolidated subsidiaries are deemed compliant.
  - Interim approach: Method stands until sector-wide guidance is issued.
  - Exclusions: The Group does not verify minimum safeguards for retail real estate customers.
- Additional notes: The text references Commission Notice C/2024/6691 for methodology; one sentence on retail credit is truncated.

nodes.title: METHOD OF ASSESSING COMPLIANCE WITH MINIMUM SAFEGUARDS
nodes.heading: METHOD OF ASSESSING C OMPLIANCE WITH MINIM UM SAFEGUARDS
nodes.start_phrase: The verification of compliance with the minimum safeguards specified in Article 18 of the EU Taxonomy by non - financial and finan cial enterprises subject to Directive 2013/34/EU is based on data obtained from the Notoria ESG Module database and information contained in the non -financial reports of these customers.
nodes.summary:
- Presents PKO Bank Polski Group’s approach to EU Taxonomy disclosures for 2024, including a consolidated key performance indicator calculated as a revenue-weighted average across segments (banking and asset management), with leasing and factoring treated like lending.
- Confirms the Group is not a financial conglomerate; taxonomy disclosures follow a prudential consolidation approach and the Commission Notice (EU) C/2024/6691 methodology.
- Describes scope, data sources, and limitations: entities subject to Directive 2013/34/EU identified via company non-financial reports, the Notoria ESG Module, and the EMIS platform to map parent–subsidiary structures and compile financed subsidiaries.
- Details minimum safeguards verification (Article 18): uses Notoria ESG data (e.g., OECD violations) and companies’ non-financial reports; applies expert judgment to assign YES/NO; if a parent meets safeguards, all its consolidated subsidiaries are assumed to meet them; banks do not verify safeguards for retail real estate customers per EC guidance and the Sustainable Finance Platform.
- Explains taxonomy eligibility/alignment assessment for exposures to financial and non-financial entities under the Directive using disclosed Turnover and CapEx KPIs (2024 reports for 2023 data), with a hierarchy: subsidiary KPI; if unavailable, closest parent KPI; if still unavailable, consolidated group KPI; for financial institutions, apply at parent level.
- For banking book exposures with unknown use of proceeds, taxonomy-eligible/aligned amounts are calculated as gross carrying amount multiplied by the relevant KPIs; earmarked financing not reported as aligned due to insufficient technical screening data.
- Addresses off-balance-sheet items: financial guarantees not disclosed due to immateriality; exposures related to managed assets via a Group subsidiary and other off-balance exposures to non-financial entities are assessed using Turnover and CapEx KPIs.
- Classifies household renovation loans as taxonomy-eligible but not aligned due to lack of technical screening evidence.
- Classifies residential mortgage exposures as taxonomy-eligible and potentially aligned if they meet substantial contribution to climate change mitigation and DNSH for adaptation (activity 7.7), evidenced by energy performance certificates.
- Provides national thresholds for energy performance: for buildings before 31 Dec 2020, EP < 83.91 kWh/(m2*yr) single-family and < 81.86 kWh/(m2*yr) multi-family; for buildings after that date, EP at least 10% below NZEB limits (63 and 58.5 kWh/(m2*yr) respectively) per Polish regulations.

nodes.title: ASSESSMENT OF ELIGIBILITY FOR AND ALIGNMENT WITH THE TAXONOMY OF EXPOSURES TO FINANCIAL AND NON-FINANCIAL ENTITIES SUBJECT TO DIRECTIVE 2013/34/EU
nodes.heading: ASSESSMENT OF ELIGIBI LITY FOR AND ALIGNME NT WITH THE TAXONOMY OF EXPOSURES TO FIN ANCIAL AND NON -FINANCIAL ENTITIES S UBJECT TO DIRECTIVE 2013/34/EU
nodes.start_phrase: To determine the exposure to financial and non - financial entities subject to Directive 2013/34/EU and their subsidiaries consolidated by the parent company of a given capital group, classified as taxonomy -eligible and taxonomy -aligned, the Bank used key performance indicators (KPIs) of Turnover and CapEx.
nodes.summary:
- Scope and context: Excerpt from PKO Bank Polski Group’s 2024 Director’s Report detailing EU Taxonomy eligibility and alignment assessments across exposures, with regulatory interpretations and data sources.

- Minimum safeguards and documentation:
  - Institutions should obtain documentation from producers to confirm compliance with technical qualification criteria for goods/services to retail customers, but this does not apply to real estate purchases.
  - The Sustainable Finance Platform indicates households are not subject to minimum safeguards; therefore, banks need not collect minimum-safeguards information from households for mortgages or similar financing.

- Methodology for entities subject to Directive 2013/34/EU:
  - Taxonomy eligibility and alignment assessed using Turnover and CapEx KPIs disclosed in 2024 for 2023 non-financial reports.
  - Subsidiary treatment: apply the KPI disclosed by the parent for that subsidiary; if unavailable, use the closest parent’s KPI; if still unavailable, use the group’s consolidated KPI. All subsidiaries consolidated by the parent are assumed included. For financial institutions, apply at the parent level.
  - For banking book exposures with unknown purpose (loans, advances, debt securities, equity instruments), taxonomy-eligible/aligned values are calculated as gross carrying amount multiplied by the relevant Turnover/CapEx KPI.
  - Earmarked financing not reported as taxonomy-eligible/aligned due to insufficient data confirming compliance with technical screening criteria.
  - Off-balance-sheet guarantees linked to taxonomy-aligned financing are not disclosed due to immateriality.
  - Managed assets aligned with the taxonomy relate to a group subsidiary; off-balance-sheet exposures to non-financial entities under the Directive are assessed via Turnover/CapEx KPIs.

- Household exposures and taxonomy assessment:
  - Renovation loans to households are taxonomy-eligible but not aligned due to lack of evidence of compliance with technical screening criteria (sections 7.2–7.6 of Annex I to Delegated Regulation (EU) 2021/2139).
  - Residential property loans can be taxonomy-eligible and aligned if they meet substantial contribution to climate change mitigation and comply with “do no significant harm” for climate change adaptation (section 7.7 of Annex I).
  - National interpretation (Poland) for substantial contribution thresholds:
    - Buildings constructed before 31 Dec 2020: EP (non-renewable primary energy demand) must be below 83.91 kWh/(m2*year) for single-family and below 81.86 kWh/(m2*year) for multi-family, evidenced by an energy performance certificate.
    - Buildings constructed after 31 Dec 2020: EP must be at least 10% lower than the national NZEB threshold; the bank applies reduced limit values of 63 kWh/(m2*year) for single-family and 58.5 kWh/(m2*year) for multi-family, per national technical regulations.

nodes.title: ASSESSMENT OF ELIGIBILITY FOR AND COMPLIANCE WITH THE TAXONOMY OF EXPOSURES TO HOUSEHOLDS

nodes.summary:
- The report details PKO Bank Polski’s application of the EU Taxonomy to its exposures, clarifying that households are not subject to minimum safeguards; therefore, the bank does not collect minimum-safeguard data from retail clients for mortgages or similar financing.
- Methodology for entities under Directive 2013/34/EU: taxonomy eligibility and alignment are assessed using Turnover and CapEx KPIs disclosed in 2024 for 2023. A hierarchy applies KPIs from the subsidiary, nearest parent, or consolidated group; for financial institutions, KPIs are applied at the parent level.
- For banking book exposures with unknown use of proceeds (loans, debt securities, equity), taxonomy-eligible/aligned values are calculated as gross carrying amount multiplied by the relevant KPI(s).
- The bank did not report earmarked/specialized financing as taxonomy-eligible/aligned due to insufficient data to confirm technical screening criteria; financial guarantees were not disclosed due to immateriality. Managed assets exposures via a subsidiary were assessed using the same KPI approach. Off-balance exposures to non-financial entities use Turnover/CapEx KPIs.
- Households:
  - Renovation loans: taxonomy-eligible but not aligned because technical screening evidence is lacking (EU 2021/2139 sections 7.2–7.6).
  - Residential property loans: taxonomy-eligible and potentially aligned under section 7.7 if substantial contribution to climate change mitigation and DNSH for adaptation are met.
  - Energy performance criteria: 
    - Buildings before 31 Dec 2020: EP <83.91 kWh/(m²*year) for single-family; <81.86 for multi-family, confirmed by EPC.
    - Buildings after 31 Dec 2020: EP at least 10% below NZEB thresholds (63 kWh/(m²*year) single-family; 58.5 multi-family), confirmed by EPC.
  - DNSH for adaptation verified via KLIMADA 2.0 physical risk analysis, requiring risk <0.75 over the loan’s maturity.
  - Vehicle loans: not reported as taxonomy-eligible due to lack of detailed asset data (section 6.5).
- Local governments: the bank’s model is not focused on public housing; it does not disclose exposures financing public housing and did not report taxonomy-eligible specialized lending due to insufficient project-level data.
- Repossessed real estate collateral: no such exposures reported.
- Green Asset Ratio (GAR) drivers: the largest contribution comes from household residential real estate and general corporate exposures to non-financial enterprises (assessed via published KPIs), primarily supporting the climate change mitigation objective. Building alignment checks follow section 7.7 of EU 2021/2139.
- Non-reported taxonomy-aligned areas due to data gaps: targeted corporate financing (project-level), household renovation loans, household vehicle loans, and specialized lending to local governments.
- Strategy and compliance integration: the 2025–2027 Strategy sets a goal to be the leading financier of Poland’s energy transition (>20% market share), focusing on low-emission energy, low-emission buildings, and zero-emission vehicle financing.
- Climate commitments: net-zero across all scopes by 2050, with near-term actions including reducing own emissions via infrastructure/efficiency (Scope 1) and sourcing at least 90% of electricity from renewables (Scope 2).

nodes.start_phrase: In the credit portfolio classification principl es adopted by the Bank's Management Board in the first half of 2024, the Bank distinguished two classes of exposures that finance activities in the fields of environmental protection, social policy, and corporate governance.
nodes.summary:
- Strategic transition target: cover over 50% of the credit portfolio with client transformation plans by end-2027 (Scope 3 financed emissions).
- Product and partnership expansion to support the EU Green Deal: adjusting offerings (including green guarantees with Korporacja Ubezpieczeń Kredytów Eksportowych S.A.) to help clients manage rising energy costs and regulatory change and to channel capital toward climate neutrality, resilience, biodiversity protection, circular economy, and sustainable water/marine use.
- Governance and classification updates (June 2024): revised Principles of classification of sustainable development financing introducing a uniform product classification aligned with the EU Taxonomy and the European Green Bond framework; ongoing implementation in business, reporting, and IT systems.
- New sustainable finance products (October 2024 onward): launch of Sustainability-Linked Loans for syndicated corporate financing per SLL Principles; work underway on additional sustainable products for corporate, business, and enterprise segments.
- Minimum safeguards due diligence (December 2024): new regulation to assess clients’ and counterparties’ compliance with minimum safeguards (anti-corruption, taxation, fair competition, science/tech/innovation, human and labor rights); planned integration into internal banking processes.
- EU Taxonomy operationalization (2024): rollout of taxonomy questionnaires to test technical screening criteria in targeted financing; bank support for client analyses; data used to calculate Green Asset Ratio (GAR) and Banking Book Taxonomy Alignment Ratio (BTAR); ongoing flagging of eligible/aligned/supporting/transition/specialized finance exposures and enhancement of ESG data infrastructure and IT tools for expanding reporting needs.
- Internal portfolio classification: 
  - Light green (supporting sustainable development; positive environmental/social impact; included in BTAR; linked to Article 9 objectives).
  - Dark green (taxonomy-aligned per Article 3; included in GAR).
- Growth ambition: increase the share of taxonomy-aligned and supporting-sustainable-development loans, including SLLs, SLBs, eco-friendly loans (RES, electromobility, energy-efficient real estate), and “Własny Kąt” green mortgages aligned with the Green Covered Bond Framework; quantitative details referenced in capital adequacy disclosures (Template 10).
- Energy sector disclosures: reporting of exposures to nuclear and fossil gas activities using both CapEx KPI and Turnover KPI approaches for entities under Directive 2013/34/EU, covering stock KPIs and 2024 flow (new originations):
  - CapEx-based: nuclear R&D (NO); construction/operation of new nuclear (YES); operation of existing nuclear (YES). Fossil gas electricity, CHP, and heat generation (all YES).
  - Turnover-based: nuclear R&D (NO); new nuclear (NO); existing nuclear (YES). Fossil gas electricity, CHP, and heat generation (all YES).

nodes.summary: Introduces PKO Bank Polski’s E1.SBM-3 framing of climate risk as a cross-cutting ESG risk managed within the bank’s broader risk management framework, with particularly significant impact on credit risk. Citing the Risk Management Strategy of PKO Bank Polski S.A. and Group, it defines ESG factors (environmental, social, governance; negative ones as ESG risk factors) and ESG risk (negative financial consequences for the bank from ESG factors affecting customers, counterparties, or balance sheet). For sustainability reporting and portfolio assessment, the bank adopts CRR III–aligned definitions of environmental physical risk (negative financial impacts from physical environmental factors) and transition risk (negative financial impacts from the transition to a sustainable economy) on counterparties and invested assets.

nodes.title: Summary of the results of the materiality analysis in relation to climate change
nodes.heading: Table 80. Summary of the results of the materiality analysis in relation to climate change
nodes.start_phrase: IDENTIFIED MATERIAL IMPACTS RISKS OPPORTUNITIES IMPACTS RISKS OPPORTUNITIES
nodes.summary:
- Provides additional and voluntary EU Taxonomy disclosures, noting that around 65% of exposures are to taxonomy-non-eligible activities for both Turnover and CapEx KPIs.
- Extends taxonomy eligibility/alignment assessment to non-financial enterprises not covered by Article 8, using bilateral data collection in lending and newly implemented taxonomy questionnaires (launched in 2023).
- In 2024, assessed 104 investment loans totaling PLN 3,947 million: PLN 3,892.4 million taxonomy-eligible and PLN 54.6 million non-eligible.
- Among executed transactions, 43 loans totaling PLN 2,706.4 million meet substantial contribution to climate change mitigation and the DNSH principle, financing wind and solar PV, passenger rail and maritime/coastal transport, energy-efficient real estate, high-efficiency bioenergy cogeneration, and innovative material recovery from waste.
- The Bank lacks information on minimum safeguards for these borrowers; exposures are classified as “light green” (supporting sustainable development) for ESG management/reporting.
- Positions climate risk as a cross-cutting ESG risk with notable impact on credit risk; integrates it into the broader risk management framework and defines ESG, physical, and transition risks in line with CRR III.
- Materiality analysis summarizes climate change mitigation, adaptation, and energy transition topics, and identifies climate-related risks spanning physical and transition categories.
- Examples of identified risks include: delays in renewable projects due to material/technology constraints; carbon price spikes and new CO2 regulations/taxes; tighter building energy standards; need for low-emission technology investments; limited managerial capability in sustainable projects; absence of corporate decarbonization strategies; and local opposition to wind/solar installations.
- Maps physical (acute and chronic) and transition risk drivers to traditional risk types (credit, market, liquidity, operational, reputational, etc.), highlighting higher impacts from floods, hurricanes, droughts, regulatory/legal changes, carbon pricing, technology transition costs, supply chain disruptions, shifts in client behavior, and reputational pressures.

nodes.title: Impact on the traditional types of risks
nodes.heading: Impact on the traditional types of risks
nodes.start_phrase: Credit Currency Interest rate Liquidity Operational Foreign currency mortgage loans Business Macroeconomic changes Models Reputational Insurance
nodes.summary:
- Focus on climate-related risks and ESG integration in PKO Bank Polski S.A. Group’s risk management, within the 2024 Director’s Report.
- Lists key transition risks and implementation challenges: materials/technology shortages for renewables, rising GHG allowance prices, new CO2/carbon tax regulations, building energy standards, need for low-emission tech investments, management gaps in CO2 reduction strategies, project execution inefficiencies, and social opposition to wind/solar near residential areas.
- Maps physical (acute: floods, hurricanes, heat waves; chronic: droughts, sea level rise) and transition risks (political/legal, technological, market, reputational, other) to traditional banking risk types, indicating identified and relative impact levels across credit, market, liquidity, operational, reputational, and insurance risks.
- Aligns risk assessment with Polish regulation (June 8, 2021) and expands 2024 materiality to include ESG/climate across credit, interest rate, liquidity/funding, FX, operational, reputational, compliance, and conduct risks.
- Liquidity/funding risk: recognizes direct ESG impact via access/cost of sustainable wholesale funding and indirect impact via stress-test deposit outflows (energy transition costs); incorporates ESG into internal capital methodology, with impact assessed as immaterial.
- Market risk: manages derivative risk via limits and stress testing; acknowledges potential ESG-related spread component in fair value corporate bonds, though current spread differentials between sustainable and other issues remain stably low.
- Notes that detailed climate risk management disclosures are provided separately in the Group’s Capital Adequacy report.
- Group entities’ ESG posture: participated in double materiality assessment; most are not yet standalone reporters or fully implementing IRO, but selected companies (PKO TU, PKO Życie) actively manage ESG/climate risks; PKO TFI applies Bloomberg ESG Score-based relative rankings and reports Principal Adverse Impact (PAI) indicators with sectoral breakdowns and data coverage.
- Climate stress testing: Bank developed a methodology based on ECB (2022) and NGFS scenarios; portfolio-level tests for the universal bank, with separate processes for insurance companies and plans to expand per evolving regulation.
- December 2024 stress test of the corporate (incl. specialized) portfolio covering 24% of exposure (mortgages excluded due to data limits) assessed physical risks (floods, droughts) and transition risks (GHG allowance price shocks, costs of low-carbon transition). Market and reputational transition risks were excluded due to quantification gaps.
- Scenario set spans acute flood (≤1 year), baseline and disorderly short-term GHG price paths (≤3 years), and long-term (2030/2040/2050) orderly, disorderly, and hot house world pathways, combining drought exposure, GHG prices, and transition investment assumptions.
- Key findings: limited physical risk impact (especially drought) on the corporate loan book; transition risks drive more material short- and long-term effects. Uncertainties include static portfolio assumptions and limits of NGFS/other forecasts.
- Application: results inform hypothetical ESG stress tests for determining the ESG-related credit spread component in fair value corporate bond portfolios and are intended for future integration into credit policy.
- Insurance subsidiaries (PKO TU, PKO Życie) executed PFSA-designed climate stress tests across five scenarios (including two to 2050), covering physical (hail, floods, hurricanes, higher mortality) and transition risks (equity price declines in high-emission sectors, price drops in energy-inefficient properties), aligned with NGFS Below 2°C and Hot House World pathways.

nodes.title: Impact of climate physical risk on the Bank's loan portfolio
nodes.heading: Table 81. Impact of climate physical risk on the Bank's loan portfolio
nodes.start_phrase: SCENARIO TIME HORIZON PHYSICAL RISKS TRANSITION RISKS DATA SOURCES GENERAL ASSUMPTIONS
nodes.summary:
- Focus: Climate risk management and transition planning within PKO Bank Polski S.A. Group, covering stress testing of banking and insurance portfolios, key findings, limitations, and the Group’s newly adopted Transition Plan.

- Bank climate stress testing (Dec 2024):
  - Scope: Corporate credit portfolio (incl. specialised financing), 24% of portfolio as of 31 Dec 2023; mortgages excluded due to data gaps; LGD climate impact under analysis.
  - Risks/modeling: Physical (floods, droughts) and transition (policy/legal via GHG allowance prices; technology transition costs). Market and reputational transition risks not quantified.
  - Scenarios: Acute flood (≤1 year); near-term baseline and disorderly (≤3 years) driven by GHG price paths; long-term NGFS-based Orderly, Disorderly, and Hot House World (2030/2040/2050) with differing policy timing, warming limits, and risk balances.
  - Results: Limited physical risk impact (especially prolonged drought) on the corporate portfolio; transition risks materially affect ratings, PD, and ECL in both short and long term.
  - Uncertainties: Static portfolio assumption; limitations of NGFS and other forecasts.
  - Use of results: Feeding hypothetical ESG stress tests to attribute an ESG credit spread for corporate bonds at FV; planned integration into credit policy.

- Insurance stress testing (PKO TU and PKO Życie):
  - Conducted per PFSA Office methodology; five qualitative/quantitative scenarios incl. two to 2050; physical (hail, floods, hurricanes, mortality) and transition (equity declines in high-emission sectors, price drops of energy-inefficient properties).
  - Long-term assumptions aligned with NGFS Below 2°C and Hot House World.
  - Outcomes: No breach of SCR/MCR; results embedded in risk management, planning, product decisions, reinsurance structures, investment strategy, and financial plans.

- Gaps/limitations:
  - No assessment of the Group’s ability to align strategy/business model to climate change across time horizons.
  - Upstream value chain risks not included in resilience analysis.

- Transition Plan for climate change mitigation (adopted 24 Feb 2025):
  - Aim: Support Paris Agreement 1.5°C goal; cover own operations and financed emissions (scope 3).
  - Targets/objectives: Net-zero by 2050; reduce scope 1–2 emissions and source ≥90% renewable energy; improve building energy efficiency; support customer energy efficiency (scope 3).
  - Initial focus: Set scope 1–2 targets for the Bank first (Bank = 75.6% of Group emissions; Ukrainian subs ~5% constrained by wartime; remaining 19.4% are Polish subs, some in Bank-owned buildings).
  - Loan portfolio prioritization: Based on environmental impact (exposure share and emissions intensity), sector decarbonisation potential (policy/programs, economics, barriers), and market practices/tools.
  - Priority sectors selected: Energy generation and residential real estate (residential targets for PKO Bank Polski S.A. and PKO Bank Hipoteczny S.A.; energy generation for the Bank). These sectors represent >42% of the Group’s loan portfolio by gross carrying amount.
  - Next steps: Refine financed-emissions methodologies, improve data quality, and expand sectoral targets over time; periodic plan review and scope expansion.

nodes.summary:
- The document discusses stress testing of insurance subsidiaries (PKO TU and PKO Życie) under PFSA methodologies; no adverse outcomes (no breach of SCR/MCR). Results are integrated into management, risk, planning, product, reinsurance, investment, and strategy decisions.
- It notes gaps: the Group’s ability to align strategy/business model to climate change across time horizons has not been assessed, and upstream value chain risks were not included in the resilience analysis.
- A Group Transition Plan for climate change mitigation was adopted on 24 February 2025 to align with the Paris 1.5°C goal, covering own operations (scopes 1–2) and financed emissions (scope 3 loan portfolio).
- Strategic sustainability objectives include net-zero by 2050, ≥90% renewable electricity, improved building energy efficiency, and customer support for energy efficiency.
- Emissions focus: the Bank accounts for 75.6% of Group emissions; 5% come from Ukrainian subsidiaries (operating under wartime constraints); 19.4% from Polish subsidiaries, some in Bank-owned properties—so building actions at the Bank also cut subsidiaries’ emissions. Initial own-operations targets are set for the Bank, consistent with strategy.
- Sector prioritization for financed emissions targets was based on portfolio share and emissions intensity, sector decarbonization potential (policy, programs, economics, barriers), and market practices/available pathways.
- Two priority sectors selected: energy generation and residential real estate (mortgages). Targets apply to PKO Bank Polski S.A. and PKO Bank Hipoteczny S.A. for mortgages; energy sector targets apply to the Bank. Initial focus is on highest-emitting exposures; these two sectors represent over 42% of the Group’s loan portfolio by gross carrying amount. Methodologies and data quality will be refined, with expansion to additional key sectors over time.
- Resource allocation for 2025–2027 actions is in early stages and not fully completed; the Transition Plan will be reviewed and expanded progressively.
- Own operations decarbonization follows the CRREM 1.5°C pathway, focusing on real estate energy performance and fleet electrification. Key levers: purchasing Guarantees of Origin to cover ≥90% of electricity, choosing lower-emission energy/heat suppliers, selling vacant properties, space optimization and building modernization, and replacing combustion vehicles with low-emission/electric models.
- Actions already undertaken include GO purchases, property modernization/thermal upgrades, space optimization (e.g., Flexidesk), supplier ESG surveys, and fleet renewal (233 hybrids added in 2024; 323 hybrids total by year-end 2024). Plans call for scaling to ~140 projects/year, ongoing sales of vacant properties, and extending initiatives to all Group entities from 2025.
- Financed emissions targets (based on IEA and CRREM pathways; subject to methodological updates):
  - Electricity generation and supply: base intensity 1,349 kg CO2e/MWh (2023); 47% intensity reduction by 2030; 1.98% share of loan portfolio; trajectory aligned with IEA 1.5°C.
  - Residential property (mortgages): base intensity 58.8 kg CO2e/m2 (2023); 31% intensity reduction by 2030; 45.64% share of loan portfolio; approaching CRREM 2°C by 2030 with a target of CRREM 1.5°C over the longer term.

Group" aimed at supporting the achievement of the long -term objective of the Paris Agreement —making efforts to limit the temperature increase to 1.5°C above pre -industrial levels.
nodes.summary: PKO Bank Polski S.A. Group’s Management Board adopted its Transition Plan on 24 Feb 2025 to align with the Paris Agreement 1.5°C goal, covering both own operations (Scopes 1–2) and financed emissions (Scope 3 loan portfolio). The Plan targets net-zero by 2050, ≥90% renewable energy sourcing, improved building energy efficiency, and support for customers’ energy efficiency. Initial targets focus on the Bank, which generates 75.6% of Group emissions (Ukrainian subsidiaries 5% under wartime constraints; Polish subsidiaries 19.4%, some in Bank-owned properties benefiting from building measures). Priority lending sectors were selected via analysis of portfolio share and emissions intensity per PLN 1m, the Group’s national emissions financing share, sector decarbonization potential (policies, programs, economic and legal/technological factors), and market practices/tools. Energy generation (targets apply to the Bank) and residential real estate (targets apply to PKO Bank Polski S.A. and PKO Bank Hipoteczny S.A.) were chosen first, covering over 42% of the Group’s gross loan portfolio. Actions are planned for 2025–2027, with ongoing work to refine financed-emissions methodologies, improve data quality, expand to additional sectors, and complete resource allocation; the Plan will be periodically reviewed and broadened.

nodes.start_phrase: The trajectory for reducing the Bank’s own emissions has been developed in line with the CRREM 1.5°C pathway, focusing on emissions reductions in the managed real estate portfolio and the gradual replacement of company vehicles with low -emission or electric models.
nodes.summary:
- Focus of this section: PKO Bank Polski S.A. Group’s 2024 Director’s Report outlining the early-stage Transition Plan, with actions for 2025–2027 aligned to the Bank’s Strategy, covering own operations decarbonization and loan portfolio targets.
- Resource status: Full financial and resource allocation for planned initiatives is not yet completed due to the early implementation stage.

Own operations
- Decarbonization pathway: Aligned with CRREM 1.5°C, targeting managed real estate and fleet electrification/low-emission replacement.
- Key levers:
  - Purchase guarantees of origin (GOs) to cover at least 90% of electricity consumption.
  - Choose electricity and heat suppliers based on emissions intensity.
  - Optimize and modernize property portfolio; sell vacant assets; reduce space usage.
  - Replace combustion-engine vehicles with low-emission/electric models.
- 2024 actions and progress:
  - Continued GO purchases.
  - Real estate modernization and thermal upgrades; space optimization (e.g., Flexidesk) reducing portfolio size.
  - Fleet transition: 233 vehicles replaced with hybrids in 2024; 323 hybrids in total by year-end.
  - ESG survey introduced for new suppliers.
- Next steps (short- to medium-term):
  - Scale energy-saving and space-optimization initiatives to about 140 projects annually.
  - Gradual sale of vacant properties.
  - From 2025, extend initiatives to all Group entities.

Loan portfolio
- Target-setting approach: Sector screening led to prioritizing electricity generation/supply and residential real estate (mortgages). Further work planned to refine financed-emissions methodologies, improve data quality, and expand targets to additional sectors.
- GHG intensity targets (baseline 2023):
  - Electricity generation and supply:
    - Baseline intensity: 1,349 kg CO2e/MWh.
    - Target: 47% reduction by 2030.
    - Portfolio share (2023): 1.98%.
    - Trajectory: IEA 1.5°C.
  - Residential property (mortgages):
    - Scope: 1 and 2.
    - Baseline intensity: 58.8 kg CO2e/m2.
    - Target: 31% reduction by 2030.
    - Portfolio share (2023): 45.64%.
    - Trajectory: Approach CRREM 2°C by 2030; long-term target CRREM 1.5°C.
- Caveat: Changes to calculation methodologies or scenarios (IEA/CRREM) may require restatement of emissions or revisions to targets.

  - “General Policy on High-Emission Energy Sectors” aligns with Group strategy to reduce “dirty” energy exposure; approved by Management Board and published internally.
- ESG risk tolerance:
  - Strategic limit set by the Credit Committee: ratio of loans to high-emission sectors to total assets.
  - As of 31 Dec 2024: 0.13% (down from 0.19% in 2023); tolerance ≤1.6% for both the Bank and the Group.
  - Monitored quarterly and reported to the Management Board.

nodes.title: POLICIES RELATED TO CLIMATE CHANGE MITIGATION AND ADAPTATION [E1-2]
nodes.heading: POLICI ES RELATED TO CLIMAT E CHANGE MITIGATION AND ADAPTATION [E1-2]
nodes.start_phrase: The Bank's Group has two policies for managing impacts and opportunities [IRO: I30, I7, O17 ] in the area of climate change: the High -Emission Policy and the Renewable Energy Sources (RES) Policy (neither of which include exclusions).
nodes.summary:
- Focus: Climate-related disclosures, policies, actions, and risk management across PKO Bank Polski S.A. Group in 2024.

- Other disclosures:
  - No analysis of locked-in greenhouse gas emissions conducted.
  - EU Taxonomy reporting (per Delegated Regulation 2021/2178) covers financed exposures only; own investment costs and OPEX are excluded, so published KPIs cannot be linked to the Transition Plan.
  - The Group is not excluded from EU Paris-aligned Benchmarks.

- Policies on climate mitigation and adaptation:
  - High-Emission Policy (2019; tightened 2020) to systematically reduce exposure to coal/lignite extraction and coal-based power generation, covering coal-related sectors and non-RES power activities; amendments via the Bank’s Credit Committee.
  - Renewable Energy Sources (RES) Sector Financing Policy (2020; collateral/repayment expanded 2022) to increase RES financing, prioritizing PV farms and wind but open to other RES projects; implemented by the Credit Committee.
  - PKO Leasing S.A. adopted a parallel “General Policy on High-Emission Energy Sectors” (2019), aligned with Group strategy.
  - No specific policies for other identified climate-related impacts/risks/opportunities; these are managed through credit risk processes, regulatory risk monitoring, HR, and product development.
  - Green bond opportunity addressed by adding green issuance options to the Bank’s bond prospectus (updated August 2024).
  - ESG risk tolerance limit set as loans to high-emission sectors as a share of total assets, with a ≤1.6% limit for both Bank and Group; actual 0.13% as of 31 Dec 2024 (down from 0.19% in 2023), monitored quarterly and reported to the Management Board.

- Actions and resources:
  - Implemented EU Taxonomy questionnaires in January 2024 for targeted financing alignment checks.
  - Ongoing work to build an internal ESG knowledge center and customer ESG data/analytics, integrate climate stress test results into credit policy, develop ESG-inclusive credit risk models, and comply with EBA ESG Risk Management Guidelines.
  - Environmental risk reporting cadence: Sustainability Statement (annual), Capital Adequacy disclosure (semiannual), ICAAP review (annual), Credit Risk Report (quarterly).
  - Internal monitoring includes monthly tracking of light/dark green exposures, portfolio GHG by PCAF asset classes, energy performance (EP) for real estate–secured loans, and quarterly sector emission intensity per EU 2022/2453.

- Operational footprint and energy measures:
  - Energy-use reduction via space optimization (e.g., Flexidesk), efficient lighting/automation, energy and heat system upgrades, building thermal modernization, and deployment of micro-PV and heat pumps.
  - Elimination of coal-fired boilers in owned properties; some oil systems replaced with gas or connected to district heating.

- Emissions performance and targets:
  - Utilized real estate already performing below the CRREM 1.5°C pathway in 2024.
  - Electricity represents ~60% of emissions; purchase of Energy Origin Guarantees (cogeneration in 2020; RES in 2021–2023) substantially lowered market-based Scope 2 emissions.
  - Approx. 99% reduction in market-based emissions in 2024 vs. 2019.
  - Fleet transition underway (~300 low-emission vehicles replaced); further replacements, low-emission criteria for branch locations, and rollout of an Energy Management System with real-time building monitoring are planned.
  - Target to keep market-based emissions at or below 18,000 tCO2e by 2030.

- Capacity and financing:
  - Strong capital position and advanced technology/analytics support emissions monitoring, risk assessment, process optimization, and sustainable lending growth.
  - No current estimates of required capex/opex for ongoing or planned climate actions.

nodes.title: ACTIONS AND RESOURCES IN RELATION TO CLIMATE CHANGE POLICIES [E1-3]
nodes.heading: ACTIONS AND RESOURCES IN RELATION TO CLIMATE CHANGE P OLICIES [E1-3]
nodes.start_phrase: In January 2024, the Bank implemented taxonomy questionnaires, which are crucial for assessing compliance with the technical screening criteria of the EU Taxonomy in targeted financing.
nodes.summary:
- Focus area: actions, resources, governance, metrics, and targets for climate change mitigation and adaptation within PKO Bank Polski S.A. Group.
- EU Taxonomy alignment: taxonomy questionnaires launched in Jan 2024 to assess technical screening criteria in targeted financing; uniform classification of sustainability financing introduced in June 2024 to identify taxonomy‑contributing activities, reviewed annually and overseen by the Sustainable Development Committee.
- Risk management: ongoing work to embed climate into credit policy (including climate stress test results), build ESG‑aware credit risk models, create an internal green‑technology knowledge hub and ESG data analytics, and comply with EBA ESG Risk Management Guidelines.
- Reporting cadence for environmental risks: Sustainability Statement (annual), capital adequacy disclosures (semiannual), ICAAP review (annual), and Credit Risk Report (quarterly).
- Internal monitoring: monthly tracking of “light green/dark green” exposures, portfolio GHG per PCAF classes, and real‑estate energy performance; quarterly sectoral emissions intensity per EU 2022/2453 formula 3.
- Operational decarbonization measures: space optimization (e.g., Flexidesk), energy‑efficient lighting and automation, energy/heat systems upgrades, thermal modernizations, micro‑PV and heat pumps; elimination of coal boilers and replacement of some oil systems with gas or district heating.
- Emissions performance and methods: electricity ~60% of emissions; purchase of Energy Origin Guarantees (cogeneration in 2020; RES 2021–2023) led to ~99% reduction in electricity‑related emissions vs 2019 (market‑based); real estate performance already below the CRREM 1.5°C pathway in 2024.
- Additional initiatives: renewal of ~300 company cars with low‑emission vehicles; further fleet replacement, emission‑based site selection for branches, Energy Management System and real‑time building efficiency monitoring; target to keep market‑based emissions ≤18,000 tCO2e by 2030.
- Strategy 2025–2027 commitments: cover >50% of the credit portfolio with a transition plan (scope 3) by end‑2027; deploy advanced analytics for CO2 prediction and monitoring; update environmental risk provisions in credit policies; reduce own scope 1–2 emissions, improve building energy efficiency, and support clients’ energy efficiency (scope 3).
- Products and capital: developing transition/adaptation products (not all fully EU‑Taxonomy‑aligned); strong capital and advanced technology support emissions analytics, risk assessment, and lending capacity; no current estimates of required capex/opex for actions.
- ESG in operational risk: since Q4 2023, ESG (including climate) factors included in internal operational risk reports, covering physical risks (extreme events, long‑term changes) and transition risks (policy/market shifts, prohibited financing, or environmental damage).
- Data challenges: ongoing work to systematize ESG data acquisition, especially for physical risk and clients’ emissions, to enable ESG risk management and prudential reporting.
- Targets (scope 1 and 2, GHG Protocol): net‑zero by 2050; interim caps—2025 ≤27.8 ktCO2e (~71% below base year; ~14% below 2023) and 2030 ≤26.8 ktCO2e (~72% below base year; ~17% below 2023).
- Cross‑references: KPIs per Commission Delegated Regulation (EU) 2021/2178 in section 13.2.1; loan‑portfolio transition measures detailed in the Transition Plan; climate‑related strategic objectives to follow in the next chapter.

nodes.title: TARGETS RELATED TO CLIMATE CHANGE MITIGATION AND ADAPTATION [E1-4]
nodes.heading: TARGETS RELATED TO CL IMATE CHANGE MITIGAT ION AND ADAPTATION [E1-4]
nodes.start_phrase: In line with the Bank’s Strategy for 2025 -2027 and its goal of achieving net -zero by 2050 for scope 1 and 2 emissions, a CO 2e Emissions Reduction Trajectory has been developed for scope 1 and 2 until 2050.
nodes.summary:
- Focus on ESG integration and climate strategy within PKO Bank Polski S.A. Group’s 2024 Director’s Report, aligned with EU regulations (Commission Delegated Regulation (EU) 2021/2178) and the Bank’s 2025–2027 strategy.
- Strategic commitments:
  - Cover >50% of the credit portfolio with client transition plans by end-2027 (scope 3).
  - Deploy new technologies for predictive analysis and CO2 measurement/monitoring; update environmental risk provisions in credit policies.
  - Reduce own emissions (scopes 1 and 2), improve building energy efficiency, and support customers in energy efficiency (scope 3).
- Introduction (June 2024) of Group-wide Principles for classifying sustainability financing:
  - Aligned with international standards and regulatory expectations; enables identification of taxonomy-relevant lending contributing to climate mitigation and adaptation.
  - Annual review; oversight by the Sustainable Development Committee; Management Board sets risk framework; business units manage specific ESG risks and their operational risk impacts.
- Product development to support transition and climate adaptation, noting not all offerings are fully EU Taxonomy-aligned (catalogue in the Adequacy Report as of 31 Dec 2024).
- ESG risk integration into operational risk reporting from Q4 2023:
  - Physical risk: impacts from extreme events and long-term environmental changes.
  - Transition risk: negative environmental impacts tied to client activities or prohibited financing; operational events causing environmental damage.
  - Ongoing work to enhance ESG data acquisition, particularly for physical risk exposures and client emissions.
- Climate targets [E1-4]:
  - Net-zero ambition by 2050 for scopes 1 and 2; CO2e reduction trajectory established to 2050.
  - Base year 2019 emissions: ~96.87 ktCO2e.
  - Targets: 2025 ≤27.8 ktCO2e (~71% vs base; ~14% vs 2023), 2030 ≤26.8 ktCO2e (~72% vs base; ~17% vs 2023), 2050 ≤19.0 ktCO2e (~81% vs base).
  - Levers: fleet electrification/low-emission vehicles, real estate optimization and modernization, elimination of vacant properties, alignment with national decarbonization pathways (increasing electricity share, coal phase-out by 2040, heating electrification), and 1% annual emissions reduction guidance.
  - Physical risk scenario analysis conducted to identify vulnerable locations.
  - Annual review of weather and heating degree days in emissions reporting; 2019 base year maintained.
  - Loan portfolio decarbonization targets addressed in the Transition Plan section.
- Sustainable finance and capital markets:
  - Identified opportunities in green bonds; first green senior unsecured bonds issued under EMTN in Sept 2024.
- Energy consumption and mix [E1-5]:
  - Group energy use reduced by 4% in 2024.
  - Reporting approach: time-lagged data for heating fuels, generators, and purchased heat/electricity (Q4 2023–Q3 2024); actual meter readings favored, estimates used where needed; vehicle fuel on full calendar-year actuals.
  - Renewable electricity: purchases verified via Guarantees of Origin; self-generation from 28 PV installations (2024 output 695,942 kWh; 560,469 kWh self-consumed, remainder sold).

nodes.title: ENERGY CONSUMPTION AND MIX [E1-5]
nodes.heading: ENERGY CONSUMPTION AN D MIX [E1-5]

- Outlines PKO Bank Polski S.A. Group’s Scope 1 and 2 decarbonisation pathway using 2019 as the base year (96.87 kt CO2e), targeting 26.8 kt CO2e by 2030 and ≤19.0 kt CO2e by 2050 (~81% reduction).
- Describes planned reduction levers: electrifying/heavily reducing internal combustion vehicle fleet, real estate optimisation (eliminating vacant space, modernisation), heating electrification, and reliance on national energy transition trends (1% annual emissions reduction, higher electricity share, coal phase-out by 2040).
- Notes internal climate-risk work limited to physical risk scenario analyses and the annual consideration of weather/heating degree days; base year for Scope 1–2 remains unchanged.
- Highlights energy management results for 2024: total energy consumption 196,649.81 MWh (-4% y/y); fossil energy 125,089.34 MWh (-6% y/y); renewables 71,560.47 MWh (+2% y/y) representing 36% of total. No nuclear or biomass inputs reported.
- Details renewable sourcing: 71,000 MWh of purchased renewable electricity backed by Guarantees of Origin; on-site PV at 28 installations produced 695,942 kWh, with 560,469 kWh self-consumed and the balance sold.
- Explains reporting approach: heating fuels, district heating, electricity and generator diesel reported with a Q4 2023–Q3 2024 time lag; vehicle fuels reported on a full calendar-year basis; actual meter readings preferred, with floor-space-based estimates when needed.
- States the Group has no operational activities in sectors with significant climate impacts.
- Presents 2024 GHG inventory:
  - Scope 1: 12,571.73 tCO2e.
  - Scope 2: 67,029.32 tCO2e location-based; 26,238.21 tCO2e market-based.

nodes.title: GROSS SCOPES 1, 2, 3 AND TOTAL GHG EMISSIONS [E1-6]

nodes.summary:
- Energy use and mix: Total energy consumption in 2024 was 196,649.81 MWh (-4% y/y). Fossil energy was 125,089.34 MWh (64% of total; share down from 66% to 64%). Renewable energy totaled 71,560.47 MWh (+2% y/y), including 71,000 MWh purchased GoO electricity and 560.47 MWh self-generated (+147% y/y). No nuclear use. The Group reports no operations in sectors with significant climate impacts.

- Own GHG emissions (GHG Protocol): 2024 Scope 1 = 12,571.73 tCO2e; Scope 2 location-based = 67,029.32 tCO2e; market-based = 26,238.21 tCO2e. By country, emissions are overwhelmingly in Poland; by gas, Scope 1 comprised mainly CO2 with small CH4, N2O and some HFCs.

- Scope 3 (own operations) categories reported: Cat. 1, 2, 3, 5, 6, 7, 11, 13, 15. Selection driven by quantitative significance and potential for reduction; categories 4, 8, 9, 10, 12 deemed not applicable; franchise data (cat. 14) being developed.

- Scope 3 (excluding portfolio) results: 2024 total 166,852.34 tCO2e. Main contributors: capital goods 132,130.93; employee commuting (incl. remote work) 14,546.47; fuel- and energy-related activities 10,829.71; business travel 1,259.14; purchased goods and services 3,938.58; downstream leased assets 3,266.88; use of sold products 873.68; waste 6.96. Data vs. estimate shares provided per category.

- Methodology and data: Calculations per GHG Protocol, using internal spreadsheets. Organizational boundary: operational control. Real estate energy data covers Q4 2023–Q3 2024; fuels for cars and selected Scope 3 on calendar year. Emission factors from national sources (URE, KOBIZE), international databases (World Bank, AIB, DEFRA, ecoinvent), manufacturers, and industry sources.

- Emissions intensity: 0.61 thousand tons per PLN 1 million of net revenue for both location- and market-based Scope 2 methods; revenue used PLN 41,451 million.

- Instruments and schemes: 71 GWh of renewable GoOs purchased (36% of Group consumption). The Group is not in the EU ETS; regulated scheme emissions are 0%.

- Portfolio emissions – Scope 3 category 13 (leasing via PKO Leasing incl. Prime Car Management): Methodology aligned with PCAF and Polish Leasing Association guidance. 2024 financed emissions total 4,253,448 tCO2e (+29% y/y) on PLN 23,442m gross carrying amount; intensity 181 tCO2e/m PLN (up from 150). Breakdown: vehicle leasing 2,996,544; machinery/equipment excl. RES 1,235,698; RES equipment 1,624; commercial real estate 19,582. Primary-data share overall 11%.

- Portfolio emissions – Scope 3 category 15 (loans and investments across PCAF classes): 2024 financed emissions 20,825,862 tCO2e (vs. 10,995,465 in 2023), gross carrying amount PLN 355,103m; intensity 59 tCO2e/m PLN overall (67 excluding sovereign debt). The rise reflects inclusion of sovereign debt (6,944,216 tCO2e), method refinements for corporate groups, and higher use of client-reported data. Asset-class detail provided (business loans, listed equity/bonds, project finance, CRE loans, mortgages, motor vehicle loans, sovereign debt). Primary-data share 59%.

- Total Group emissions 2024: Market-based total 25,284,972 tCO2e (location-based 25,325,763). Biogenic emissions not identified (own ops) and not included in portfolio (per PCAF). Base year is 2019 for own emissions; 2023 for portfolio (cats. 13B, 15). Financed emissions are consistent across LB/MB totals.

- Trends and targets: 2024 y/y changes—Scope 1 -10.1%; Scope 2 LB -11.3%, MB -9.4%; significant Scope 3 +76.4% due mainly to portfolio scope expansion. Milestones for 2025/2030/2050 noted; sectoral decarbonization plan referenced in the Transition Plan.

- No GHG removals, carbon-credit-funded mitigation, or internal carbon pricing.

- ESRS E1-9: The Group uses Annex C exemption; no disclosure of anticipated financial impacts from climate risks/opportunities this year.

- Social information – Own workforce (intro): No particularly vulnerable groups identified; policies managed via internal regulations, not consulted with social partners; generally no ESRS 2-aligned measurable targets unless otherwise stated.

OWN WORKFORCE  
RELEVANT SUSTAINABILI TY MATTERS

stated. The main mechanism for counteracting negative impacts is the adoption of internal regulations. The adopted
