nodes.title: CHARACTERISTICS OF EMPLOYEES
nodes.heading: CHARACTERIS TICS OF EMPLOYEES
nodes.start_phrase: The predominant form of employment in the Bank as well as in the Bank's Group is an employment contract.
nodes.summary:
- Workforce profile and contract types: 96.54% of Group staff (25,884 people) are employed under employment contracts; 3.5% (927) work under civil law contracts. Among those on employment contracts, 71.11% are women. No employment outside Poland exceeded 10% of total headcount. Gender reporting covers women and men only (no other/undisclosed gender identified in 2024).
- Gender representation and leadership: Women form the majority of employees and hold 62.85% of middle-management and 56.27% of director-level roles. Women account for 31.10% of Material Risk Takers (MRTs).
- Headcount structure by age, job group and MRTs (Group): Other employees 22,179; middle management 1,957; managers 1,539; MRTs 209. Age bands used: up to 30, 30–50, above 50, with the bulk of staff in the 30–50 range across job groups.
- Working hours and contract terms (Group): 25,311 full-time and 573 part-time employees; contract terms reported as 3,374 “permanent” and 22,510 “indefinite period.”
- Inclusion and disability: Employment policy emphasizes equal treatment and diversity across gender, age, health, orientation, religion, marital status, and origin. People with disabilities represent 1.5% of Group staff (391 employees; 72.6% women).
- Turnover and mobility: 2024 Group turnover rate was 10.1% (women 10.0%, men 10.2%). Departures totaled 2,590 (71.1% women). New hires totaled 2,733 (10.6% of headcount), with women at 67.7%. Internal transfers within the Group are not counted as exits/entries at Group level.
- ESRS reporting scope: The Group used transitional provisions in 2024 for own-workforce indicators covering non-employee workers (S1-7), social protection (S1-11), training and skills (S1-13), and work-life balance (S1-15).
- Remuneration governance: A Group-wide “Remuneration Policy for Employees of the Bank and the Bank’s Group,” adopted/updated by the Management Board, aligns subsidiary systems (notably for management board members and MRTs), links pay to results via objective criteria, is publicly accessible internally, and is supported by regular market benchmarking and salary reviews.
- Collective Labour Agreements (CLA): In force at PKO Bank Polski S.A. and KREDOBANK S.A. (with trade unions); other Group companies do not have CLAs. CLA components include basic salary; additional pay for overtime, night work, and hazardous conditions; and bonuses/awards for special achievements.

nodes.title: REMUNERATION
nodes.heading: REMUNERATION
nodes.start_phrase: The source document regulating remuneration issues within the Bank's Group is the "Remuneration Policy for Employees of the Bank and the Bank's Group" adopted and updated by the Management Board.
nodes.summary:
- Workforce changes in 2024: The Group hired 2,733 people (10.6% of total employment), with women comprising about 68% of new hires at both the Bank and Group levels; internal transfers within the Group are excluded from these figures.
- ESRS transitional period: The Group used transitional provisions for selected own-workforce indicators (S1-7 non-employee workers, S1-11 social protection, S1-13 training and skills, S1-15 work-life balance).
- Remuneration governance: A Group-wide Remuneration Policy sets consistent, market-aligned, results-based pay rules for the Bank and subsidiaries, including management boards and Material Risk Takers; it is publicly accessible and supplemented by regular market analyses and salary reviews.
- Collective Labour Agreements (CLA): In force at PKO Bank Polski S.A. and KREDOBANK S.A.; define pay components (basic salary, premiums for overtime/night/hazardous work, bonuses/awards) and guarantee minimum basic pay linked to statutory minimum wage and job classification. CLAs cover employees on employment contracts (not management/civil contracts); application in foreign branches may vary due to local law. Ongoing dialogue with unions and employee councils supports stability and working conditions.
- Bonus systems and benefits: The Bank operates Employee Bonus Rules tying goals to key management indicators; a Social Benefits Fund provides financial aid (e.g., grants for hardship/unforeseen events), and an Employee Pension Scheme is available. Subsidiaries maintain their own remuneration regulations and bonus schemes, with additional tools like project or holiday bonuses and wage advances.
- Monitoring and targets: Financial security and pay adequacy are monitored via eNPS (with a focus on the remuneration and benefits index); while no formal ESRS2 target is set, the aim is to maintain scores at least at 2023 levels.
- Adequate wage: All Bank and Group employees in 2024 received pay above the defined adequate wage threshold (0% below), determined using national minimum wage references (Poland: GUS; Ukraine: Budget Code).
- Pay gap approach: The remuneration policy is gender-neutral; salaries are set through job valuation using market methodology and objective criteria (e.g., skills), with the section continuing beyond the provided excerpt.

nodes.title: ADEQUATE WAGE
nodes.heading: ADEQUATE WAGE
nodes.start_phrase: The Bank's Group strives to ensure that employees receive adequate remuneration that meets the needs of the employee and their family, taking into account the national economic and social conditions.
nodes.summary:
- Collective Labour Agreement (CLA): Guarantees minimum basic salary as a percentage of statutory minimum wage by job classification; covers all Bank employees on employment contracts (excludes management contracts/civil law agreements). Applies to foreign branches subject to local conditions; at KREDOBANK S.A. it covers all employees. No specific targets set, but ongoing dialogue with unions and the Employee Council on working conditions and job stability.

- Bonus and benefits: Bank-wide Employee Bonus Rules (excluding Material Risk Takers) link goals to key management indicators; rules set processes for goal-setting and bonus calculation but no specific targets or monitoring. Social Benefits Fund provides additional benefits, including non-repayable grants for hardship (applications can be made by the employee or colleagues). Employee Pension Scheme in place.

- Subsidiaries: Remuneration principles set in regulations and contracts; separate bonus systems. Additional financial security tools include project/holiday bonuses and wage advances.

- Monitoring: Financial security and pay satisfaction tracked via eNPS, focusing on the “remuneration and benefits” index; aim is to maintain at least the 2023 level (no ESRS2 measurable target).

- Adequate wage: Defined against national minimum wage (Poland: GUS; Ukraine: Budget Code). In 2024, 0.0% of Bank and Group employees were paid below this level.

- Gender pay approach: Gender-neutral policy based on job valuation (skills, problem solving, impact). Use of market comparability index (CR/Comparatio); internal analyses indicate women and men are paid at market levels.

- Gender pay gap results (ESRS unadjusted 2024): Bank 30.0%, Group 31.7%, driven by employment structure (more women in sales/non-managerial roles; more men in high-decision roles).

- Adjusted gender pay gap (controls for job family, job evaluation level, geography): Bank 2.3%, Group 3.8%; methodology aligned with the Polish Bank Association; indicates no unjustified pay inequalities.

- Calculation scope/methods: Metrics based on total 2024 pay (annualised, FTE-adjusted) for active employees on the last day of the year; includes Management Board; excludes hires after September 30; adjustments for partial-year employment and unpaid leave.

- Pay ratio: Highest total remuneration to median employee remuneration in 2024—Bank: 18.2; Group: 18.7 (calculated on the same population and basis).

nodes.title: PAY GAP
nodes.heading: PAY GAP
nodes.start_phrase: The Bank's remuneration policy is gender -neutral.
nodes.summary:
- Remuneration and job valuation:
  - Positions are valued based on skills, problem-solving, and impact on results; valuation applies to roles, not individuals.
  - Regular salary reviews consider internal benchmarks and external remuneration data.
  - The Bank uses a market comparability index (CR/Comparatio) to benchmark pay; internal analyses show no differences between women’s and men’s pay relative to the market.

- Gender pay gap (2024):
  - Unadjusted gender pay gap (ESRS method): Bank 30.0%; Group 31.7%.
  - Employment structure drives the unadjusted gap (more women in sales/non-managerial roles; more men in high decision-making roles).
  - Adjusted gender pay gap (controls for job family, job evaluation level, and location): Bank 2.3%; Group 3.8%.
  - Methodology: averages calculated within homogeneous groups; overall indicator is a headcount-weighted average; Group includes subsidiaries weighted by their employee counts; aligned with Polish Bank Association approach.
  - Conclusion: adjusted gap indicates no unjustified pay inequalities; differences reflect organizational structure.

- Pay ratio (2024):
  - Ratio of highest total remuneration to median employee remuneration: Bank 18.2; Group 18.7.
  - Calculations include total remuneration paid in 2024, annualized and FTE-adjusted; include Management Board; exclude employees hired after September 30, 2024; consider active employees on the last day of the year.

- Training and development:
  - Group encourages continuous employee development; actions taken by entities across the Group (no Group-wide regulation, but Bank-level regulation outlines processes).
  - Internal regulation “Organisation and Implementation of Development Activities at PKO Bank Polski S.A.” details organization of individual and group development for employees.
  - 2024 activities included workshops (in-person/online), video training, educational games, VR, and ~20 new e-learning courses; topics spanned communication, collaboration, time/work management, change, negotiation, stress/emotion management, presentation, motivation, creativity/innovation, and self-development.
  - Key initiatives/resources:
    - “Knowledge in a Nutshell” knowledge-sharing by employees.
    - Multilife platform (language learning, Legimi, Youniversity).
    - Application Zone for hard skills (Excel, SQL, Python, PowerPoint).
    - Language Zone (platform access, English meetings, webinars, reading recommendations via Legimi/Inspiro).
    - Training Catalogue (workshops, video trainings, short formats).
    - “Inspirational Development Time” for regional sales staff.
    - Monthly “Time for Development” live events.
  - Group companies offer soft skills and specialist training, e-learning platforms, language courses (often funded), study funding, knowledge bases, tailored training, webinars, and guides.
  - Monitoring: no ESRS-aligned targets; effectiveness tracked via eNPS “Development” index; 2024 goal to maintain at least near 2023 levels.

- Future skills focus:
  - Ongoing evolution of training to support environmental objectives; employees serving high-emission sectors and clients under decarbonization plans will upskill to deliver professional advisory during the transition.

nodes.title: TRAINING AND DEVELOPMENT
nodes.heading: TRAINING AND DEVELOPM ENT
nodes.start_phrase: The Bank's Group actively supports and encourages employees to continue their development and strives to meet the growing demand for development and training activities.
nodes.summary:
- Focus areas: employee training and development; workplace safety and ergonomics across PKO Bank Polski S.A. Group in 2024.
- Training and development:
  - No group-wide regulation; entities run their own competence-building initiatives.
  - Bank-level framework: “Organisation and Implementation of Development Activities at PKO Bank Polski S.A.” outlines access and organization for individual and group development (internal/external training), without ESRS-aligned targets.
  - Broad development offer delivered via workshops (in-person/online), educational games, VR, video training; ~20 new e-learning courses added in 2024.
  - Skills covered: communication, collaboration, personal effectiveness, time/work management, change, negotiation, stress/emotion management, presentations, motivation, creativity/innovation, self-development.
  - Additional initiatives: Knowledge in a Nutshell (peer-led knowledge sharing); Multilife platform (language, Legimi, Youniversity); Application Zone (Excel, SQL, Python, PowerPoint); Language Zone (platform, English meetups, webinars, book recs via Legimi/Inspiro); Training Catalogue; Inspirational Development Time (regional sales network); monthly Time for Development live events.
  - Subsidiaries offer soft skills/specialized training, e-learning platforms, language courses (with funding), study funding, knowledge bases, tailored training, knowledge capsules, webinars.
  - Monitoring via eNPS “Development” index; no measurable 2024 targets, aim to keep near 2023 levels.
  - Upskilling planned for employees serving high-emission sectors to support client decarbonization and transition advisory.
- Safety and ergonomics:
  - No group-wide OHS management system; all entities comply with national regulations and maintain their own rules.
  - Bank’s key OHS document sets responsibilities and provisions for PPE, workwear, eyewear reimbursement, and covers employees, contractors, interns, trainees, and third-party staff on premises.
  - Measures include periodic inspections, OHS and first aid training (mandatory/voluntary), ergonomic assessment of new job positions, and post-setup reviews.
  - Subsidiary examples: ergonomic guidance within policies (e.g., Health, Safety and Environmental Protection Policy; remote work OHS instructions).
  - Accident prevention through OHS training, updated risk assessments, periodic audits, and incident analysis.
  - 2024 outcomes: zero fatalities; recordable accidents—Bank 56 (rate 1.56), Group 60 (rate 1.27); recordable work-related ill health—Bank 0, Group 3; days lost—Bank 1,102; Group 1,179. Accident rate methodology based on reportable accidents per 1,000,000 hours; Group rate averaged due to incomplete hours data.
  - Employee well-being supported through non-regulated initiatives, including flexible work arrangements (remote work and individual schedules) to improve work-life balance.

nodes.title: SAFETY AND ERGONOMICS AT WORK
nodes.heading: SAFETY AND ERGONOMICS AT WORK
nodes.start_phrase: Ensuring a safe working e nvironment plays a significant role within the Bank's Group.
nodes.summary:
- Focus on workplace safety and ergonomics across PKO Bank Polski S.A. Group, with OHS managed at the entity level rather than group-wide; compliance with national regulations but no OHS system based on international standards.
- Bank’s core OHS rulebook defines responsibilities, PPE/workwear/beverages/vision reimbursement, and applies to employees, contractors, interns, trainees, and external workers on premises; managerial duty to organize compliant workplaces.
- Practical OHS measures: periodic inspections, compliance checks, mandatory and voluntary OHS/first aid training, evaluation of new positions by OHS services during setup and post-arrangement; similar practices in selected subsidiaries.
- Ergonomics guidance formalized in certain subsidiaries (e.g., TU and PTE policies and remote work OHS instructions); otherwise derived from Polish Labour Code and general OHS regulations.
- Accident prevention occurs without a dedicated policy via training on hazards, ongoing occupational risk assessment updates, periodic condition inspections, and accident cause analyses.
- 2024 safety outcomes: zero fatalities (injuries or ill health) at Bank and Group; recordable accidents—Bank 56 (rate 1.56), Group 60 (rate 1.27); recordable work-related ill health—Bank 0, Group 3; days lost—Bank 1,102; Group 1,179. Accident rate methodology based on hours worked (group rate averaged due to incomplete hour data).
- Employee health and well-being initiatives: flexible work (remote work, individual schedules), hybrid model maintained widely despite return-to-office trends, two additional vacation days for timely full annual leave use.
- Health programs in 2024: customizable medical packages; specialist consultations, vaccinations, diagnostics, hospital care, rehabilitation; prevention drives (e.g., “2 Hours for Health Prevention,” annual check-ups); Health Days with dietitians/physiotherapists/VR stress relief and fitness tests; “health sensor” app; #FokusNaCiebie wellbeing platform; stress/burnout/relationship webinars; sports clubs and integration activities; similar offerings in subsidiaries.
- Monitoring of well-being and satisfaction via eNPS (well-being and satisfaction indices); aim to maintain results at least at 2023 levels; no ESRS2-style measurable target set.
- Employee data security supported by Bank-level Security Policy and Information Protection Rules; no separate group regulation. Potential impact of trust loss from data incidents assessed as possible but not widespread/systemic; no corrective actions undertaken.
- Social dialogue and employee representation: active cooperation with employee bodies; full respect for freedom of association per ILO Convention No. 87; no obstacles to union or council participation; organizations free to self-govern.
- Bank’s employee representation includes three trade unions: National Trade Union of PKO BP S.A. Employees; “Solidarity” Independent Self-Governing Trade Union of PKO BP S.A. Employees; and Inter-Company Organisation for Banking and Service Employees No 06-005 OPZZ “Confederation of Labour.”

nodes.title: COOPERATION WITH OWN WORKFORCE, INCLUDING COLLECTIVE BARGAINING AND SOCIAL DIALOGUE [S1-2]
nodes.heading: COOPERATION WITH OWN WORKFORCE , INCLUDING COLLECTIV E BARGAINING AND S OCIAL DIALOGUE [S1-2]
nodes.start_phrase: Cooperation with the social side is an important channel essential for understanding the employees' perspective, learning their opinions, and using this information in business operations.
nodes.summary:
- Focus on employee wellbeing and work-life balance: two additional vacation days for timely use of full statutory leave; maintenance of hybrid work models with significant remote work across the Group despite market trends toward office return.
- Comprehensive health and prevention programs: customizable health packages for employees and families; expanded medical care (specialists, vaccinations, diagnostics, hospital care, rehabilitation); preventive actions like “2 Hours for Health Prevention” and annual exams; Health Days with experts, VR stress-relief, and fitness tests; a “health sensor” app; #FokusNaCiebie wellbeing platform; webinars on stress, burnout, and relationships; integration and sports clubs. Similar measures implemented in subsidiaries.
- Monitoring of wellbeing outcomes: regular eNPS surveys focusing on “well-being” and “satisfaction,” with an aim to maintain results at least at 2023 levels; no measurable ESRS2 target set.
- Employee data security: managed via internal “Security Policy” and “Rules for the Protection of Information” adopted by the Management Board; documents available internally. The risk of loss of employee trust due to data loss/theft is identified as potential but not widespread/systemic; no corrective actions taken.
- Social dialogue and collective bargaining (S1-2): active cooperation with employee representatives; full respect for freedom of association in line with ILO Convention No. 87; no obstacles to joining unions or the Employee Council; unions self-govern and elect their representatives freely.
- Employee representation: three trade unions operate at the Bank—The National Trade Union of PKO BP S.A. Employees; “Solidarity” Independent Self-Governing Trade Union of PKO BP S.A. Employees; Inter-Company Organisation for Banking and Service Employees No. 06-005 OPZZ “Confederation of Labour.”

nodes.title: EMPLOYEE REPRESENTATION AND FREEDOM OF ASSOCIATION
nodes.heading: EMPLOYEE REPRESENTATI ON AND FREEDOM OF AS SOCIATION
nodes.start_phrase: Understanding the role of dialogue, the Bank actively collaborates with employee representatives within its framework.
nodes.summary:
- Work-life balance and work model:
  - Two additional vacation days for timely use of full statutory annual leave.
  - Hybrid work model maintained across the Group with significant remote work despite market trends to return to offices.

- Employee health and wellbeing:
  - Comprehensive health benefits for employees and families (specialist consultations, vaccinations, diagnostics, hospital care, rehabilitation).
  - Preventive initiatives (“2 Hours for Health Prevention,” annual check-ups), Health Days with experts and VR stress-relief, a health sensor app, #FokusNaCiebie wellbeing platform.
  - Webinars on stress, burnout, relationships; sports and integration programs; similar solutions in subsidiaries.
  - Monitoring via eNPS “well-being” and “satisfaction” indexes; objective to maintain results at least at 2023 levels (no ESRS2 measurable goal).

- Employee data security:
  - Governed by PKO Bank Polski S.A. Security Policy and Rules for Protection of Information; documents available internally.
  - Risk of loss of employee trust due to data loss/theft assessed as potential, not widespread/systemic; no corrective actions undertaken.

- Social dialogue, representation, and collective bargaining:
  - Full respect for freedom of association in line with ILO Convention No. 87; no obstacles to unionization or Employee Council activity.
  - Three trade unions operate at the Bank; cooperation governed by the Labour Code and Trade Union Act (23 May 1991).
  - Employee Council elected by staff; term ends 22 August 2026; formal cooperation agreement provides information rights (within 7 days) and access to employer resources.
  - Employer informs on employment situation, staffing levels and changes, and measures affecting work organization or employment terms; unions receive necessary information upon request.
  - Dedicated communication via INTRA portal (“Dialogue and Employee Representation”); Social Labour Inspection active on rights and OHS.
  - Bank fulfills statutory duties to inform/consult/agree with social partners and engages them on broader business matters.

- Roles and responsibilities:
  - Directors of Employee Relations Division and HR Partnership Department authorized for collective labour law actions, negotiations (including disputes), and statutory information duties, including consultations with the Employee Council.
  - HR Partnership Director coordinates cooperation with unions and the Employee Council.
  - Director of Organisational Culture and Engagement oversees employee/candidate experience and opinion surveys.

- Group-wide employee dialogue:
  - Communication adapted to entity size/specificity (direct contact, email, intranet); mechanisms to report labour rights violations.
  - Key subsidiaries (e.g., PKO Bank Hipoteczny, KREDOBANK, PKO Faktoring, PKO Leasing, PKO Ubezpieczenia, PKO TFI, Prime Car Management, PKO Finat) conduct eNPS to assess employer–employee cooperation.
  - Focus on promoting social dialogue and freedom of association without formal targets.

- Internal communication and workplace climate:
  - Emphasis on effective internal communication and a positive atmosphere; no formal policies or targets—addressed through available initiatives.
  - Intra/portal as primary information hub across the Group.
  - eNPS surveys (#JakCiSięPracuje) used to analyze team relations and align HR strategies; complemented by employee meetings and onboarding.

- Inclusion, diversity, and generational initiatives (#JestemUSiebie):
  - Program fosters an inclusive environment through communications, education, and workshops (neurodiversity, unconscious bias including gender roles, nonviolent communication).
  - Mandatory diversity and inclusion e-learning; ongoing webinars, podcasts, and microlearning.
  - Support for returning parents (#PonownieUSiebie): guidance for employees/managers, webinars, “Back in the Bank” sessions, and moderated “Parental e-coffee.”
  - Age diversity actions: workshops on empathetic leadership for Gen Z and effective intergenerational dialogue.
  - Activities align with the Diversity Charter; recurring #Rotunda Różnorodności event on diversity, tolerance, anti-discrimination, and inclusive workplace building.

nodes.title: INTERNAL COMMUNICATION AND WORKING ATMOSPHERE
nodes.heading: INTERNAL COMMUNICATIO N AND WORKING ATMOSP HERE
nodes.start_phrase: The Bank's Group actively promotes eff ective internal communication, aiming to ensure a high level of employee satisfaction and create a supportive environment with a positive atmosphere.
nodes.summary:
- Employee relations and social dialogue: The Group uses eNPS surveys (including #JakCiSięPracuje) to assess cooperation and workplace relationships, promotes social dialogue and freedom of association through various initiatives, but has no formal objectives or required actions set in this area.

- Internal communication and workplace atmosphere: No dedicated policies or targets, but extensive use of internal portals (Intra and company intranets) to share information on rights, benefits, and responsibilities. Survey insights are used to strengthen team communication and align HR strategies. Employee satisfaction is supported by meetings and onboarding.

- Inclusion and diversity (#JestemUSiebie): A comprehensive program building an inclusive culture via communication, education, workshops, and mandatory e-learning on diversity and inclusion (biases, neurodiversity, nonviolent communication). Additional resources include webinars, podcasts, and short learning modules.

- Support for parents (#PonownieUSiebie): Reboarding support for employees returning from parental-related leaves, including guidelines for staff and managers, a Bank-wide webinar on returning to work, “Back in the Bank” welcome sessions, and moderated “Parental e-coffee” exchanges.

- Age diversity: Targeted workshops such as “Empathetic Leadership for Generation Z Managers” and “Intergenerational Dialogue” to improve cross-generational communication, motivation, and collaboration. Actions align with the Diversity Charter; the Bank hosts the recurring #Rotunda Różnorodności event on diversity, tolerance, and anti-discrimination.

- Employee opinion surveys across the Group: Regular surveys with varying scope by company and contract type (employment, civil law, cooperation, B2B), used to identify improvement areas and drive organizational development and satisfaction.

- Human rights: No group-level human rights policy explicitly referencing UN/ILO/OECD standards; instead, rights are embedded in internal documents compliant with legal standards. Covered areas include dignity, freedom of expression and belief, privacy, equal treatment, access to information and healthcare, rest, safe working conditions, fair pay, freedom to enter employment, and professional development.

- Governance instruments: Respect for human rights codified in the Code of Ethics, Anti-Mobbing and Anti-Discrimination procedures, Work Regulations, Remuneration Policy, and Recruitment Policy, with implementation across numerous subsidiaries. Work Regulations emphasize dignity, equal treatment, anti-discrimination, safety and hygiene, rest, employment of young workers, and employee familiarization with rules.

nodes.title: HUMAN RIGHTS
nodes.heading: HUMAN RIGHTS
nodes.start_phrase: The Bank's Group has not adopted a human rights policy at the group level.
nodes.summary:
- Employee opinion surveys: Conducted regularly across PKO Bank Polski Group entities, with scope tailored by contract type per company (employment, civil law, B2B, cooperation). Purpose is to gather feedback, identify improvement areas, and enhance organizational development and employee satisfaction.

- Human rights approach: No group-level human rights policy referencing UN/ILO/OECD; instead, compliance is embedded in internal documents aligned with international and national law. Covered rights include identity, expression, personal rights, equal treatment, access to information and healthcare, privacy, rest, safe/hygienic conditions, fair pay, freedom to enter employment, and professional development.

- Key internal regulations:
  - Code of Ethics: Promotes respect, dignity, diversity, and prevention of unequal treatment; implemented across multiple subsidiaries.
  - Work Regulations: Ensure dignity, equal treatment, access to information, anti-discrimination and anti-mobbing, safe work conditions, rest, and rules for employing young workers; applied at the Bank and subsidiaries; all employees have access and are informed.
  - Employee Remuneration Policy: Group-wide framework to ensure fair remuneration.
  - Recruitment Policy: Standardizes objective, non-discriminatory selection; guarantees equal treatment and gender neutrality; mandates diversity goals for managerial hires; subsidiaries expected to align.

- Accessibility: All regulations available in an internal regulatory database for all employees.

- International alignment: Adheres to principles consistent with Global Compact and OECD Guidelines; no framework agreement with employee representatives on human rights.

- Managing impacts: Human rights violations’ potential impacts on employee health are mitigated through existing practices; no separate policy; impacts are not widespread/systemic. Reporting channels are available to employees and external parties.

- Forced and child labor: No operations identified with significant risk; compliance grounded in applicable legal prohibitions.

- Mobbing and discrimination: No separate group-wide diversity/equal opportunity policy; risks addressed through the Code of Ethics, Work Regulations, and a Management Board-approved procedure for counteracting mobbing/discrimination and handling employee rights complaints; explicit protection across multiple characteristics and employment types.

nodes.title: MOBBING AND DISCRIMINATION
nodes.heading: MOBBING AND DISCRIMIN ATION
nodes.start_phrase: The Bank's Group does not have a policy aimed specifically at eliminating discrimination (including harassment), promoting equal opportunities, and other methods of enhancing diversity and social inclusion at the Group level.
nodes.summary:
- Focus on human rights management across the PKO Bank Polski S.A. Group, including:
  - Group-wide Employee Remuneration Policy ensuring fair pay.
  - Recruitment Policy based on objective, non-discriminatory criteria, gender neutrality, and diversity goals for managerial roles.
  - Internal access to all regulations via a shared database.
  - Alignment with international initiatives (UN Global Compact, OECD Guidelines); no framework agreement with employee representatives.
  - Human rights impacts on employee health mitigated through existing practices; risks assessed as potential, not widespread or systemic.
  - No identified significant risks of forced or child labor, relying on applicable legal prohibitions.

- Mobbing and discrimination:
  - No single group-level DEI policy, but application of internal regulations: Code of Ethics, Principles for Counteracting Mobbing and Discrimination (with complaint procedures), and Working Regulations.
  - Management duties to prevent unequal treatment; monitoring via employee satisfaction (eNPS) indicators.
  - Subsidiaries either adopt dedicated anti-mobbing/discrimination policies or apply the Bank’s Code of Ethics.
  - 2024 cases: 58 total (Bank: 54); 6 discrimination, 0 sexual harassment, 11 mobbing, 41 other (e.g., inappropriate supervisory behavior, nepotism, poor atmosphere).
  - Two compensation payments related to pre-2024 lawsuits; total financial impact for incidents/complaints: PLN 40.56 thousand.
  - Violence/harassment impact categorized as potential; not widespread/systemic.

- Diversity and inclusion commitment:
  - On 14 November 2024, the Bank signed the Diversity Charter, committing to ban discrimination, promote equality and diversity management, and engage employees and partners to foster an inclusive culture.

- Channels for raising concerns and whistleblowing:
  - Dual pathways: HR complaint process and dedicated whistleblower channels.
  - Current and former employees can file complaints on employment rights, including mobbing/discrimination.
  - Submission methods: official email (naruszenie.uprawnien.hr@pkobp.pl) or written to the HR Partnership Department.
  - Complaints handled by the Director of the HR Partnership Department; may involve cross-unit teams and legal counsel.
  - Confidential, data-minimizing process; monitoring and corrective actions by HR business partners as needed.
  - Protections: confidentiality/anonymity, anti-retaliation guarantees, option for temporary job transfer during investigations, escalation to the President of the Management Board or Supervisory Board where applicable.
  - Subsidiaries use email/written channels; KREDOBANK also offers a website interface.

nodes.title: CHANNELS FOR RAISING CONCERNS
nodes.heading: CHANNELS FOR RAISING CONCERNS
nodes.start_phrase: The employee complaint process o perates within the Bank both through HR procedures and through dedicated whistleblower channels outlined in the section on business procedures.
nodes.summary:
- Emphasis on an inclusive organizational culture where all individuals are accepted and valued.
- Comprehensive employee complaint and whistleblowing framework:
  - Applicable to current and former employees; covers violations of employment rights, including mobbing and discrimination.
  - Multiple reporting channels (electronic and written); visibility of options via the Intranet.
  - Complaints handled by the HR Partnership Department Director with possible support from other units and legal counsel.
  - Confidential investigation process; monitoring and follow-up by HR business partners.
  - Strong whistleblower protections: confidentiality, limited data processing, option to request temporary transfer, and a strict ban on retaliation; escalation paths to the President of the Management Board or the Supervisory Board.
  - Subsidiaries predominantly use email/written channels; KREDOBANK also offers a website interface.
- Consumers and end-users (retail customers) materiality overview:

nodes.title: PROTECTION OF CUSTOMER PRIVACY [IRO: I164, I165]
nodes.heading: PROTECTION OF CUSTOME R PRIVACY [IRO: I164, I165 ]
nodes.start_phrase: The Bank manages customer priv acy protection in accordance with the "Security Policy of PKO Bank Polski S.A." and the "Information Security Rules for Protected Data in PKO Bank Polski S.A."
nodes.summary:
- Focus area: Relationships with consumers and end-users (retail customers of the Bank, subsidiaries, and cooperating agencies/intermediaries).
- Materiality outcomes:
  - Five potential negative impacts: unfair communication, data loss/theft, information asymmetry, inappropriate advice, discriminatory actions (none widespread/systemic; preventative actions in place).
  - One actual positive impact: strong customer privacy protection that builds trust and elevates sector standards.
  - Six significant opportunities identified; no risks; opportunities are indirectly addressed in the current strategy. No unified policy yet for these impacts/opportunities.
- Product stance: No inherently harmful products; full product information provided. All customers are privacy-vulnerable; people with disabilities and children are especially vulnerable to marketing/sales.
- Inclusion and accessibility:
  - Needs identified via cooperation with NGOs, analysis of complaints/inquiries (including social media), and external auditors (digital).
  - Dedicated Young Customer Office and School Savings Campaign (SKO); participation in the Polish Bank Association’s interbank accessibility group.
  - Implemented branch accessibility methodology; mandatory training for new sales staff on serving persons with disabilities.

  - Governed by the Bank’s Security Policy and Information Security Rules; group-wide security standards for strategic companies; each entity acts as a separate data controller with its own policies.
  - NDAs/data processing agreements in place; agents/intermediaries contractually obliged to Bank security standards.
  - Management Board oversight; Security Department conducts audits, inspections, and reports to the Management and Supervisory Boards; group companies report under agreed guidelines.
  - Compliance with GDPR, Poland’s Personal Data Protection Act, and Banking Law; strict banking secrecy and controlled disclosures to authorized entities.
  - Incident response aligned with GDPR: prompt mitigation, notification to the data protection authority (UODO) and affected individuals when required.
  - Data Protection Officer appointed; customers informed about processing and rights (including consent withdrawal); information available on the Bank’s website; channels for GDPR-related complaints and rights requests. Privacy policy not consulted with customers.
- Complaints management:
  - No group-wide complaints policy yet (target 2026); most subsidiaries have their own rules; Bank Hipoteczny aligns with Bank provisions.
  - Comprehensive complaint system for retail customers covering all interactions; clear rules and procedures set channels, deadlines, response methods, and external dispute resolution options.
  - Complaints can be submitted by Bank and Bank Hipoteczny customers and non-customers; external institutions may intervene.
  - Customer Ombudsman appointed to handle appeals, support customers, and interface with external protection bodies.
  - Annual complaints report to the Operational Risk Committee and Management Board; no exclusions in the rules.

nodes.title: COMPLAINTS [IRO: I161, I162, I164, I165, I167, I168]
nodes.heading: COMPLAINTS [IRO: I161, I162, I164, I165, I167, I168 ]
nodes.start_phrase: The Bank does not have a Group -wide complaints policy but has initiated the process of its preparation, with implementation planned for 2026.
nodes.summary:
- Data protection and security: The Bank maintains internal security policies tailored to each entity, has appointed a Data Protection Officer (DPO) with public contact channels, and provides GDPR-compliant information on data processing, customer rights (access, rectification, erasure, consent withdrawal), and breach management and notification procedures. Policies were not consulted with customers.

- Complaints management: There is no Group-wide complaints policy yet (targeted for 2026), but the Bank operates comprehensive Rules and Procedures for handling complaints, applications, and appeals from retail customers and even non-customers. The framework sets submission channels, resolution deadlines, response methods, and extrajudicial resolution bodies, and covers Bank Hipoteczny via outsourcing. A Customer Ombudsman handles appeals, interfaces with external institutions, and issues an annual report to the Operational Risk Committee and Management Board. The Management Board holds ultimate responsibility.

- Ethical standards and non-discrimination: While there is no standalone anti-discrimination policy for customers, non-discrimination is embedded in the Bank’s Code of Ethics and the sector’s Principles of Good Banking Practice. The Code commits to respectful, unbiased treatment (including seniors and persons with disabilities) and is reviewed annually, with results reported to the Supervisory Board. The Customer Service Standards (KOS), aligned with the Code, are recommended for subsidiaries and monitored via Mystery Shopper and agency visits; analyses and recommendations are led by the Sales Quality Office.

- Accessibility and inclusion: The Bank advances accessibility for customers with disabilities and seniors through branch location and architectural adaptations (50 branches modernized in 2024; new standard from 2025), acceptance of guide/assistance dogs, Polish Sign Language service in all branches/agencies (via smartphone), individualized service including dedicated rooms, and digital accessibility of the website, online banking (iPKO), and mobile app (IKO) to WCAG 2.1 AA. Additional support includes the Talk2IKO voice assistant and staff training, aligned with national accessibility legislation.

nodes.title: PREVENTING DISCRIMINATION [IRO: I168, O79]
nodes.heading: PREVENTING DISCRIMINA TION [IRO: I168, O79 ]
nodes.start_phrase: The Bank's Group and the Bank itself do not have a formal policy aimed at preventing the discrimination of customers.
nodes.summary:
- Governance and complaints: The Management Board holds top responsibility for implementing internal Rules. Complaints and appeals are handled under the Bank’s Code of Ethics, Principles of Good Banking Practice, Code of Good Practice for Brokerage Houses, and service quality standards. Required complaint information is published online and provided to complainants.

- Non-discrimination: While there is no standalone customer anti-discrimination policy, commitments are embedded in the internal Code of Ethics and the sector’s Banking Code of Ethics. The Bank declares respect for diversity and addresses needs of seniors and people with disabilities. Compliance with ethical principles is reviewed annually by the Management Board, with results reported to the Supervisory Board. The internal Code was not externally consulted or publicly disclosed.

- Customer Service Standards (KOS): Implemented at the Bank (recommended to subsidiaries), grounded in the Code of Ethics, monitored via Mystery Shopper and dedicated monitoring, with analysis by the Sales Quality Office. Aims include improving customer satisfaction and apply without exclusions.

- Accessibility and inclusion: Broad measures to ensure equal access for customers with special needs, including:
  - Accessible branch locations and layouts; 50 branches modernized in 2024 to meet mobility accessibility, with a new arrangement standard planned from 2025.
  - Entry permitted for guide/assistance dogs; Polish Sign Language service in all branches via smartphone; individualized service in dedicated rooms.
  - Digital accessibility: website, iPKO, and IKO aligned to WCAG 2.1 AA; Talk2IKO voice assistant for manual disabilities.
  - Expanded remote and online services (more documents accepted online, remote advisory via phone/video, “selfie” account opening, online appointment booking).
  - Alternative transaction authorization (SMS, electronic signature pads with emailed copies) in all branches.
  - Integration with public digital services (Trusted Profile, e-Identity, and applications for ZUS family and disability benefits).
  - ATM accessibility: 92% equipped with audio modules; device information provided online.
  - Combating digital exclusion through self-service education and in-branch support for ATMs/deposit machines/internet stations; about 360 branches with internet stations and ~120 with dedicated Customer Assistants by end-2024.

- Financial education for youth: PKO Junior app for children under 12 to build financial habits; SKO program for primary school students, parents, and teachers, reaching around one million children.

- Privacy and cybersecurity awareness: Ongoing customer education via website, iPKO, IKO, and social media; participation in national campaigns (“Scamming Out! Stop Internet Fraud”; co-financing the Polish Bank Association’s campaign). Active media engagement by Bank experts and communication on new security features (e.g., security keys, behavioral login verification) and safe practices during high-risk shopping periods.

- Plain-language communication: Introduction in 2024 of Standards for Simple Communication with Customers, covering all customer-directed content (letters, emails, SMS, app/transactional notifications, self-service device messages, website/app content, terms and agreements, forms, brochures/marketing materials, online campaign content, and templates for inquiries/complaints).

nodes.title: COMMUNICATION - GREENWASHING [IRO: I161]
nodes.heading: COMMUNICATION - GREENWASHING [IRO: I161]
nodes.start_phrase: The Bank has implemented recommendations and guidelines regarding the accuracy and truthfulness of the information provided, product naming rules, best practices for formulating sustainability statements, including behaviors or communications that may lead to greenwashing, and the definition of sustainable financial products and services, as well as the criteria for their qualification.
nodes.summary:
- Focus on plain-language communication: standardizing customer-facing language to be simple, inclusive, and legally precise; staff training in legal design; knowledge sharing with subsidiaries; roll-out of the PKO Prosto app to support content simplification.
- 2024 implementation highlights: embedded plain language in internal regulations; 70 certified ambassadors plus recruitment of 20 more due to Accessibility Act (B2 readability); piloted a text-assessment metric; created a “B2 ecosystem” to meet the 28 June 2025 statutory requirement covering terms, agreements, forms, and admin communications.
- B2 ecosystem components: audits (31 of 130 units create content; ~1,000 B2 submissions by end-2024); ambassador team expanded in Q1 2025 (+20); Jira-based request management with PKO Prosto; cooperation with external editors; market lobbying to align B2 with plain language.
- Effectiveness metrics: average score before simplification 4.06 vs. 4.65 after (scale 1–6, ≥4 aligns with plain language); 2,417 texts simplified; 7,286,814 characters processed with 732,701 characters removed; 806 PKO Prosto users (as of 20 Feb 2025).
- Customer feedback: no formal feedback tool yet; reliance on established evidence that plain language improves experience; planned 2025 studies on accessibility impact.
- Greenwashing controls [IRO: I161]: bank-wide guidelines for accuracy, product naming, and sustainability statements; 2024 internal Decision governing external communications across the Bank, Group, and Foundation; links to new 2024 regulations on classifying sustainable financing and ESG credit portfolio reporting; clear responsibilities, evaluation criteria, consultation options, and managed deviations; 6 communications assessed in 2024; annual review of subsidiary implementation; no greenwashing lawsuits in 2024.
- Regulatory engagement [S4-4]: identification and gap analysis of sustainable finance regulation; education and workshops; participation in interbank task forces and dialogue with regulators on ESG implementation.
- Marketing communications governance [IRO: I161, O74]: internal principles define creation and approval of messages; updated from 2025 under new Principles of marketing activity with stronger measurement/analysis; requirements for reliability, clarity, and balanced presentation of benefits, costs, and risks; compliance reviews include internal units and apply to external agencies; adherence to sector codes (Bank’s Strategy 2025–2027, PBA Code of Banking Ethics, consumer credit ad standards, PFSA principles, canon of good practices); uniform standards across all customer segments; subsidiaries marketing via the Bank with prior consent; no supervisory proceedings or non-compliance cases in 2024.
- The next section header “Inadequate Advice [IRO: I162]” is introduced but its content is not included in this excerpt.

nodes.title: MARKETING COMMUNICATION [IRO: I161, O74]
nodes.heading: MARKETING COMMUNICATI ON [IRO: I161, O74 ]
nodes.start_phrase: The Bank provides customers with access to information on products and services by defining the manner in which marketing communications are created in the “Principles for the conducting of marketing and public relations (PR) activities and social communication by PKO Bank Polski S.A.”.
nodes.summary:
- Greenwashing oversight: In 2024 the Bank analyzed six communications, will review implementation of related decisions across subsidiaries annually, and recorded no greenwashing lawsuits.
- Sustainable finance/ESG compliance: The Bank maps relevant regulations, conducts legal gap analyses, monitors adaptation, runs education and workshops, participates in interbank task forces to counter greenwashing, and engages regulators on ESG implementation.
- Marketing communications governance: Communications are governed by internal principles; from 2025 rules are updated under the “Principles of marketing activity by PKO Bank Polski S.A.” with “General requirements for creating advertising messages,” and greater focus on measuring activities and assessing media partners.
- Advertising standards: Messages must be reliable, non-misleading, lawful, and fair; clearly identify the product/service; present benefits without downplaying costs/risks; and avoid any potential to mislead.
- External codes followed: The Bank aligns with its 2025–2027 Strategy, the Polish Bank Association’s Code of Banking Ethics, consumer credit advertising best practices, KNF principles for advertising banking services, and the canon of good financial market practices.
- Controls and oversight: Communications are vetted by subject-matter and compliance units; standards apply equally across all customer segments and channels; external agencies are held to the same ethics; Group subsidiaries marketing through the Bank require prior consent.
- 2024 compliance outcome: No supervisory proceedings or cases of non-compliance in marketing communications within the Bank or its Group.
- Next section indicated: Inadequate Advice [IRO: I162].

nodes.title: INADEQUATE ADVICE [IRO: I162]
nodes.heading: INADEQUATE ADVICE [IRO: I162]
nodes.start_phrase: The Bank makes every effort to manage the potential impact on customers related to improper advice.
nodes.summary:
- Governance of greenwashing and ESG: In 2024, the Group analyzed six communications for potential greenwashing, will annually review implementation across subsidiaries, and recorded no greenwashing-related lawsuits. It identifies and monitors sustainable finance regulations, conducts legal gap analyses, runs education and workshops, participates in interbank task forces, and engages regulators on ESG implementation.

- Marketing communications controls: The Bank operates under detailed internal principles for marketing and PR, updated from 2025 with new general requirements and greater focus on measuring activities and media partner due diligence. Advertising must be clear, reliable, non-misleading, and balanced on benefits, costs, and risks. The Bank adheres to sectoral codes and PFSA guidelines, consults content with expert and compliance units, applies the same standards across all segments and channels, and requires external agencies and certain subsidiaries to follow these rules. In 2024, there were no supervisory proceedings or non-compliance cases related to marketing ethics.

- Mitigating inadequate advice: Product development follows internal principles and PFSA recommendations, with reviews to ensure legal compliance and customer needs alignment. The Bank ensures transparent, accessible, and comprehensive pre- and post-contract information, prevents unfair competition and misleading ads, maintains lawful contract templates, and provides complaint mechanisms.

- Facility safety standards: The Group ensures customer and employee safety through legally compliant security systems (alarms, CCTV, access control), physical protection, and monitoring. Internal policies govern security, and subsidiaries in Bank premises follow the same standards. Employees receive e-learning and on-site training, including drills on robbery prevention and handling threats.

- Financing approach to R&D and sustainability: The Group does not earmark separate financing for companies conducting safety/health R&D but monitors exposures against the sustainable taxonomy. It is expanding financing to support clients’ energy transition (e.g., real estate, transport), enhancing societal safety and health while strengthening reputation, engagement, product uptake, and revenue.

- Customer engagement: Retail customer input is collected continuously via complaints, call center, website form, and email, with effectiveness tracked through NPS. Responsibility for improvements is decentralized to business units; the CX research team advises but does not mandate actions.

- Feedback and remediation channels: The Group gathers input through double materiality surveys, complaints, email and web forms, call center, retail customer satisfaction surveys, and on-screen and telephone surveys.

Internal regulations (Security Policy; Principles for the Protection of People and Property; Technical Security in Branches and Agencies) apply, including to Group companies using bank premises. Staff receive e-learning and in-branch training with drills on robbery prevention and response to security threats.

It is expanding financing that supports sustainable development and client energy transition (real estate, transportation), which is expected to improve societal safety/health and strengthen reputation, customer engagement, and revenues.

Effectiveness is tracked primarily through NPS. Action-taking is decentralized to business units; the CX research unit provides insights but does not direct other units’ actions.

PFSA guidance), ensuring transparent and comprehensive customer information, preventing unfair competition via honest advertising, aligning contractual templates with law, and providing avenues for complaints.

- Facility safety standards (IRO: O75): The Group ensures safe customer service through legally compliant security frameworks, modern systems (alarms, CCTV, access control), physical protection and monitoring, and uniform security standards for Group companies in Bank facilities. - Financing related to safety/health R&D (IRO: O76): The Group does not separately earmark financing for companies developing safety/health products but monitors exposures against the sustainable product taxonomy. It expands financing for sustainable development, especially clients’ energy transition in real estate and transport, improving societal safety/health while strengthening reputation, engagement, and revenues.

Effectiveness is tracked via satisfaction metrics, notably NPS. Responsibility for NPS improvements is decentralized across business units; the CX research unit advises but lacks formal authority over other units’ actions.

nodes.title: REMEDIATION PROCESSES AND REPORTING CHANNELS

nodes.start_phrase: The Bank's Group takes action to gather customer feedback through the following channels :
nodes.summary:

nodes.heading: METRICS AND OBJECTIVE S

Detailed targets, baselines, and goal levels for customer relationships tied to significant risks/opportunities are not disclosed as they are trade secrets.

The Bank and subsidiaries have management board–approved codes of ethics setting values, conduct standards, and ethical principles; the Bank’s Code applies to employees and all parties acting on its behalf, reflecting values such as partnership.

nodes.title: CORPORATE CULTURE - Introduction
nodes.heading: CORPORATE CULTURE
nodes.start_phrase: The organisation systematically shapes and promotes corporate culture by integrating values into daily operations, HR processes, and management practices.
nodes.summary: Overview of how PKO Bank Polski S.A. Group shapes corporate culture through values embedded in daily operations, HR processes, and management practices, governed at entity level without a group-wide policy. The Bank and subsidiaries operate Management Board–approved Codes of Ethics (no exemptions) covering partnership, development, and impact; commitments to local communities, social partners, anti-corruption, and environmental care; high service standards and customer interest protection; and fair supplier selection and objective information policies. The Code applies to employees and all persons acting for the Bank and addresses the “Corporate Culture” impact category (IRO: I175, I178, I179, I180, I170, O80). The Management Board conducts periodic reviews of ethical principles as a mitigating mechanism for double materiality risks (IRO: R110). Subsidiaries (e.g., PKO Towarzystwo Ubezpieczeń S.A., PKO Bank Hipoteczny S.A., PKO Leasing S.A., KREDOBANK S.A.) adopt codes based on the Bank’s and receive best practices to standardize HR. Culture-building includes assessing the current state, defining a target cultural profile with progress metrics, and embedding values in recruitment, onboarding, annual reviews, and opinion surveys. The main monitoring tool is the eNPS survey (four editions in 2024); culture is promoted via internal/external communications such as #naWARTOŚCIowane Piątki and New Leadership Sound, with 2024 live events drawing over 5,000 participants and ongoing expert-led sessions to strengthen leadership and skills.

nodes.title: IDENTIFICATION AND ASSESSMENT OF SIGNIFICANT IMPACTS, RISKS, AND OPPORTUNITIES RELATED TO CORPORATE CULTURE
nodes.heading: IDENTIFICATION AND AS SESSMENT OF SIGNIFIC ANT IMPACTS , RISKS, AND OPPORTUNITIES R ELATED TO CORPORATE CULTURE
nodes.start_phrase: In the Bank and the Group, corporate culture plays a key role in building resilience to crises, enabling the organisation to effectively adapt to a changing environment.
nodes.summary:
- Emphasis on the Bank’s Code of Ethics as the foundation of corporate culture, covering stakeholder relations, anti-corruption, environmental care, customer protection and service quality, fair supplier selection, and transparent information policies; links to double materiality impacts and Management Board oversight through periodic reviews.
- Rollout of ethics standards and HR best practices across Group subsidiaries with no exemptions, supporting consistency in values and conduct.
- Structured cultural transformation: assessment of current vs. target culture, defined progress metrics, and embedding core values into recruitment, onboarding, performance reviews, and employee surveys with cross-functional involvement.
- Measurement of engagement and value alignment via eNPS, with four survey editions in 2024.
- Internal and external culture-building communications and leadership programs (#naWARTOŚCIowane Piątki, New Leadership Sound/#NoweBrzmieniePrzywództwa), live events with 5,000+ attendees, expert-led sessions, and training to create a modern, supportive workplace.
- Identification and assessment of culture-related impacts, risks, and opportunities, highlighting culture’s role in crisis resilience; leadership maturity and inclusive culture development; values-based prevention of mobbing, harassment, and discrimination; and mental resilience training.
- Integration of sustainable development/ESG into culture through organization-wide education: live ESG events, specialist trainings (emissions, decarbonization pathways, greenwashing, climate and carbon footprint, climate competitiveness), dedicated ESG site, and mandatory e-learning; opportunity recognized but intentionally not formalized to maintain flexibility.
- Structured social impact: PKO Bank Polski Foundation with transparent, policy-based grant allocation and settlement procedures (no exclusions).
- Sponsorship and marketing/PR/social communication governed by internal rules defining scope, decision rights, and controls to mitigate operational, compliance, and reputational risks; monitoring and compliance checks embedded; rules address impacts identified in DMA for sponsorship and advertising; apply to PKO Bank Polski S.A. only, with no exclusions.
- Comprehensive reputational risk management across the Group: media monitoring, incident analysis and recording, corrective actions and public statements, internal reporting to a Reputational Events Database, and protective measures in vendor management, outsourcing, and product pre-implementation; additional internal policies at certain Group entities.
- Upcoming section signposted: Protection of Whistleblowers (content not included in this excerpt).

nodes.title: PROTECTION OF WHISTLE BLOWERS
nodes.heading: PROTECTION OF WHISTLE BLOWERS
nodes.start_phrase: The Bank's Group does not have a whistleblower protection policy implemented at the gro up level, as these matters are regulated at the level of individual entities.
nodes.summary:
- Corporate culture and resilience: The Group fosters a culture that prevents mobbing, harassment, and discrimination, and builds crisis resilience through development programs and mental resilience training. Sustainable development is integrated via education and daily practice (ESG events, e‑learning, and expert trainings on emissions, decarbonization, greenwashing, climate, and competitiveness), intentionally without formal internal regulations to preserve flexibility.

- Ethics and social engagement: Core values guide ethical conduct with customers and stakeholders. Charitable activities are carried out through the PKO Bank Polski Foundation in social assistance, health and life protection, and environmental areas, under a transparent fund allocation policy without exclusions.

- Sponsorship and marketing governance: Sponsorship supports education, civic initiatives, culture, and sports. Marketing, PR, and social communication are governed by Bank-level rules adopted by the Management Board, defining scope, decision rights, and controls to mitigate operational, compliance, and reputational risks. Activities are monitored per internal regulations and a control function matrix. These rules address DMA-identified impacts but apply only to PKO Bank Polski S.A., not group-wide.

- Reputational risk management: The Bank identifies, assesses, controls, monitors, and reports reputational risk; tracks media coverage; records incidents and losses; issues corrections/statements; and maintains a Reputational Events Database. Protective measures extend to contractor management, outsourcing, and pre-implementation product reviews. Similar internal policies apply in Group entities meeting set criteria, and the Group supports sector-wide reputation safeguarding.

- Whistleblower protection: There is no Group-level policy; regulations exist at entity level. The Bank complies with EU Directive 2019/1937 and Poland’s 2024 Whistleblower Protection Act via an internal regulation covering reporting, protections, monitoring, and remedial actions, with no exemptions. Comparable frameworks are in key subsidiaries. Since September 2024, external parties (candidates, contractors, partners) can also report via channels published on the Bank’s website. Anticipated impacts include increased trust, greater transparency through more reports, and alignment with growing policy expectations.

- Anonymous reporting: A widened whistleblowing scope covers unethical/unlawful acts, internal rule breaches, and supervisory recommendation violations. Reports can be made electronically, by phone, mail, in person, or via the encrypted Sygnanet channel. Reporters receive confidentiality and protection against reprisals; access is restricted to authorized staff; feedback is provided where feasible.

- Open reporting: Employees may submit identified reports to the Compliance Department or other units through multiple channels (electronic, letter, phone, in person). Reporters are protected, with disclosures made only when legally required; they may seek assistance from the Bank’s President in case of reprisals, and receive feedback when it does not harm Bank or third‑party interests.

nodes.title: PROTECTION OF WHISTLE BLOWERS - Introduction
nodes.heading: PROTECTION OF WHISTLE BLOWERS
nodes.start_phrase: The Bank's Group does not have a whistleblower protection policy implemented at the gro up level, as these matters are regulated at the level of individual entities.
nodes.summary: This section outlines PKO Bank Polski S.A. Group’s approach to whistleblower protection in 2024: there is no group-level policy, as rules are set by individual entities; the Bank complies with EU Directive 2019/1937 and Poland’s Whistleblower Protection Act of 14 June 2024 via an internal regulation (adopted by the responsible unit’s Director) that defines reporting of legal violations, protection measures for employees and other reporters, monitoring of non-compliance reports, and remedial actions, with no exemptions and full coverage of “Whistleblower Protection” impacts and opportunities [IRO: I187, I188, I184]. Comparable regulations are in required subsidiaries: PKO Towarzystwo Ubezpieczeń S.A., PKO Życie Towarzystwo Ubezpieczeń S.A., PKO BP Finat sp. z o.o., PKO Towarzystwo Funduszy Inwestycyjnych S.A., PKO Leasing S.A., Prime Car Management S.A., PKO Bank Hipoteczny S.A., PKO Faktoring S.A., and PKO BP Bankowy PTE S.A. Since September 2024, procedures and reporting channels are published on the Bank’s website, enabling reports from employees, job candidates, contractors, and other partners, aiming to increase employee trust [I187], discourage complaints due to lack of protection [I184], raise reported irregularities to enhance transparency [I188], and leverage the growing policy importance of whistleblower protection [O84].

nodes.title: ANONYMOUS REPORTS
nodes.heading: ANONYMOUS REPORTS
nodes.start_phrase: The Bank has internal regulations establishing a system for anonymous reporting of violations (the whistleblower framework applies to all unethical or unlawful activities, violations of the Bank’s internal regulations, as well as breaches of recommendations from supervisory and control authorities).
nodes.summary:
- Scope and context: Excerpt from the PKO Bank Polski S.A. Group Director’s Report 2024 (p. 281/288) covering whistleblower protection.
- Governance model: No group-wide whistleblower policy; rules are set at the level of individual entities.
- Legal compliance: The Bank complies with EU Directive 2019/1937 and Poland’s Whistleblower Protection Act of 14 June 2024, with an internal regulation defining reporting principles, protection measures, monitoring of non-compliance, and remedial actions; no exemptions. Impacts/opportunities addressed under IRO: I187, I188, I184, O84.
- Subsidiary coverage: Whistleblower regulations implemented in required subsidiaries, including PKO TU S.A., PKO Życie TU S.A., PKO BP Finat sp. z o.o., PKO TFI S.A., PKO Leasing S.A., Prime Car Management S.A., PKO Bank Hipoteczny S.A., PKO Faktoring S.A., PKO BP Bankowy PTE S.A.
- Public transparency and access: Since Sept 2024, procedures and channels published on the Bank’s website; reporting enabled for employees, job candidates, contractors, and other cooperating entities.
- Strategic impacts: Aims to increase employee trust (I187), deter complaints arising from lack of protection (I184), raise transparency by increasing reported irregularities (I188), and leverage the growing importance of whistleblower protection (O84).
- Anonymous reporting: System covers unethical/illegal acts, breaches of internal rules, and supervisory recommendations; scope extended to ethical and internal standard violations. Channels include electronic, phone, mail, in person, and an independent encrypted platform (Sygnanet). Strong confidentiality: identifying data removed if inferable; reporters protected from retaliation; escalation route to the President of the Management Board. Access to reports restricted to designated, authorized staff; feedback provided where possible, though anonymity may limit responses.
- Open reporting: Employees may file identified reports to the Compliance Department or other Bank units via electronic, letter, phone, or in-person (including offsite). Protection applies except for mandatory disclosures to courts/law enforcement in criminal matters; recourse to the President available; feedback provided if it does not harm the Bank or third parties.
- Reporting channels: Specific contact details are provided, including a dedicated phone line ((22) 580 25 50) and postal addresses for the Compliance Department, the President of the Management Board, and the Supervisory Board.

nodes.title: OPEN REPORTS
nodes.heading: OPEN REPORTS
nodes.start_phrase: The Bank’s employees also have the option to submit open reports of irregularities.
nodes.summary:
- Scope and context: Part of PKO Bank Polski S.A. Group Director’s Report 2024 detailing whistleblower protection and anti-corruption/bribery measures.
- Whistleblower governance: No group-wide policy; regulations implemented at entity level. The Bank complies with EU Directive 2019/1937 and Poland’s Whistleblower Protection Act (14 June 2024) via an internal regulation setting reporting principles, protections, monitoring, and remedial actions without exemptions.
- Subsidiary coverage: Whistleblower rules adopted in all required subsidiaries (e.g., PKO TFI, PKO Leasing, PKO Bank Hipoteczny, PKO Faktoring, insurance entities, etc.).
- External accessibility: Since Sept 2024, whistleblowing procedure and channels are published on the Bank’s website, enabling reports from employees, candidates, contractors, and other partners.
- Impact management: Measures aim to build trust, reduce complaints due to lack of protection, increase transparency through more reported irregularities, and leverage growing corporate emphasis on whistleblower protection.
- Anonymous reporting framework: Expanded beyond statutory scope to include ethical and internal standard violations; reports accepted via electronic, phone, mail, in person, and an encrypted platform (Sygnanet).
- Protection and confidentiality: Strong safeguards against retaliation; personal data removed if identity can be inferred; access to reports restricted to designated, authorized staff; feedback provided where possible.
- Open reporting option: Employees may report openly to the Compliance Department or other units via multiple channels; protections apply except where disclosures to authorities are legally required; feedback provided when it does not harm Bank or third-party interests.
- Governance and training: Recipients of reports hold written authorization and receive dedicated training; employees undergo mandatory initial and periodic training; policies and procedures available on the intranet.
- Oversight and reporting: Information on reports and verification outcomes is periodically submitted to the Management Board and Supervisory Board.
- Anti-Corruption Policy: Group-wide policy adopted by the Management Board, effective 2025, establishing zero tolerance for corruption, cronyism, and nepotism; entities must align internal regulations with the policy.
- Alignment and oversight: Policy supports the UN Convention Against Corruption; introduces an Anti-Corruption Compliance Officer and Board-level supervision with periodic reviews; no exemptions.
- Consolidation of prior rules: Replaces previously fragmented guidance (e.g., gift/benefits rules, Code of Ethics, compliance risk frameworks, Polish Bank Association ethics code).
- Risk and opportunity focus: Addresses reputational, legal, market integrity, and investor confidence risks (e.g., avoiding investigations/costs and anti-competitive behavior impacts).
- Implementation roadmap: Detailed procedure to start 1 April 2025, covering prevention, training, incident response, and reporting to management and supervisory bodies; no dedicated budget yet; internal communication initiated via email and standard channels.
- Investigations: No separate fast-track process for corruption cases beyond whistleblower mechanisms; reliance on existing compliance risk management, investigation, and procurement procedures.

nodes.title: PREVENTION OF CORRUPTION AND BRIBERY
nodes.heading: PREVENTION OF CORRUPT ION AND BRIBERY
nodes.start_phrase: The Anti -Corruption Policy of PKO Bank Polski S.A. and the PKO Bank Polski S.A. Group has been adopted by the Management Board and will come into effect in 2025.
nodes.summary:
- Whistleblower protection: Multiple secure reporting channels (postal with “WG” annotation, Sygnanet app, dedicated email, and direct email to the Supervisory Board Chair for Management Board matters). Strong safeguards against retaliation and strict confidentiality (including deletion of identifying data). Designated, trained recipients authorized by the President of the Management Board. Mandatory initial and periodic staff training, intranet access to procedures, and periodic reporting of irregularities to the Management and Supervisory Boards. Investigations handled by an independent Security Department, with separation of investigative and managerial functions.

- Anti-corruption and bribery: A new Group-wide Anti-Corruption Policy has been adopted (effective 2025), aligned with the UN Convention Against Corruption, with oversight by a Management Board member and an Anti-Corruption Compliance Officer. Previously dispersed rules (gifts/benefits policies, Codes of Ethics/Banking Ethics, compliance risk) will be unified. The policy targets key risks (reputation, legal/investigation costs, anti-competitive behavior, corruption scandals, investor confidence). An Implementation Procedure (from 1 April 2025) will detail prevention, training, incident response, reporting to governance bodies, and identification of higher-risk functions/units; an additional responsible unit will reinforce investigative independence. No separate fast-track for corruption cases beyond whistleblowing; reliance on compliance, investigation, and procurement procedures. Training: mandatory onboarding and periodic anti-corruption modules for all employees, tailored sessions for management/supervisory members, annual reminders on accepting benefits/gifts, and expanded programs coordinated by the Compliance Officer. In 2024 there were no corruption-related convictions or fines; no remedial actions required. No specific implementation budget yet; employees informed via internal communications.

- Political influence and lobbying: No Group-level policy; the parent company has internal rules for cooperation with political parties (account and credit rules, periodic monitoring, no exemptions; non-public), addressing risks from DMA assessments. The Group participates in public consultations with authorities, regulators, supervisors, and industry bodies. The Bank is listed in the EU Transparency Register (No. 129427193168-74) with interests including the EU Taxonomy (Reg. 2020/852), Market Abuse Regulation (Reg. 596/2014), and Capital Requirements Regulation (Reg. 575/2013).

nodes.title: POLITICAL INFLUENCE AND LOBBYING ACTIVITIES
nodes.heading: POLITICAL INFLUE NCE AND LOBBYING ACT IVITIES
nodes.start_phrase: The Bank’s Group does not have a policy regulating issues related to political influence and lobbying activities implemented at the group level.
nodes.summary:
- Anti-corruption governance and training
  - New Anti-Corruption Policy and an Implementation Procedure for PKO Bank Polski S.A. and its Group to take effect in April 2025.
  - Investigative and managerial functions are separated; investigations are handled by the independent Security Department, with further reinforcement planned via an additional responsible unit after the policy takes effect.
  - The Implementation Procedure will identify functions/departments/positions most exposed to corruption and bribery risks (not specified in the current policy).
  - Mandatory anti-corruption training is part of compliance risk management for all new employees, covering ethics, anti-corruption rules, and acceptance of benefits/gifts; periodic mandatory training will be introduced under the new policy.
  - The Anti-Corruption Compliance Officer will coordinate training initiatives; management and supervisory board training is delivered as needed; annual reminders on accepting benefits/gifts are sent; additional training is planned under the new Implementation Procedure.
  - No corruption-related convictions or fines in 2024; no remedial actions required.

- Political influence and lobbying
  - No group-level policy on political influence/lobbying; the parent company has internal regulations (non-public) governing cooperation with political parties (account opening/maintenance, credit provision, and periodic monitoring), addressing risks identified in DMA assessments.
  - The Bank and subsidiaries engage in transparent participation in public consultations with authorities and industry bodies.
  - The Bank is registered in the EU Transparency Register (No. 129427193168-74); areas of interest include the EU Taxonomy Regulation (2020/852), Market Abuse Regulation (596/2014), and CRR (575/2013).
  - In 2024, no meetings, consultation submissions, or expert group activities were recorded in the transparency register.
  - The Bank provides financing (loans) to political parties per internal rules and reported a positive balance in 2024; loans are not considered political contributions. Political contributions are prohibited and none were made in 2024.
  - No designated management/supervisory representative for lobbying or political influence; no additional related risks identified.
  - No current Management Board or Supervisory Board members held public administration positions in the two years prior to their appointment.

- Counteracting money laundering and terrorist financing (AML/CFT)
  - The Group operates under a Group AML/CFT Policy, Bank-level Rules and Procedures, and AML/CFT Strategies that define information exchange, responsibilities, and operational steps for Bank units, agents, and intermediaries.
  - Provisions apply to Group entities that are “obligated institutions” under the Polish AML Act; each obligated institution must develop its own strategy/internal regulations aligned with the Group Strategy.
  - Obligated and related entities listed include PKO Bank Hipoteczny S.A., PKO TFI S.A., PKO Leasing S.A., PKO BP Finat Sp. z o.o., PKO Życie TU S.A., PKO Finance AB, KREDOBANK S.A., Neptun – FIZAN, PKO VC – FIZAN, and indirectly KREDOLEASING Sp. z o.o., PKO Leasing Sverige AB, PKO Faktoring S.A., Prime Car Management S.A., Masterlease Sp. z o.o., Futura Leasing S.A., Bankowe Towarzystwo Kapitałowe S.A., Kompania Finansowa Prywatne Inwestycje Sp. z o.o.
  - Deadline for companies to implement their AML/CFT strategies: 18 April 2025.
  - The AML/CFT Strategy addresses legal compliance (including the EU regulatory package), governance and competency allocation for ML/TF risk management, and process enhancements.
  - No exclusions in internal AML/CFT regulations; actions are performed only by obligated institutions.
  - In 2024, the Bank aligned with EBA guidelines and the PFSA Office’s stance on compliance management and the AML/CFT compliance officer role; Group and Bank AML/CFT Strategies were adopted; all obligated entities must implement the Group Strategy and prepare internal strategies.
  - AMLCO oversees implementation and AML Act compliance; AMLRO identifies ML/TF risks and mitigation actions; mechanisms are in place to mitigate risks identified via materiality analysis.

nodes.summary:
- Identifies three entity-specific topics without a common group policy: ability to operate beyond armed conflict, product compliance, and development of industry and infrastructure.
- Ability to operate beyond armed conflict: outlines medium- to long-term opportunity to support Ukraine’s reconstruction via KREDOBANK S.A., focusing on energy, transport, housing, utilities, infrastructure, and social services once the war ends; highlights ongoing humanitarian efforts, employee safety, business continuity, and client service; notes KREDOBANK’s 2025–2027 strategy to ensure stability and prepare for reconstruction; confirms continued financing with risk mitigation through guarantees and cooperation with international institutions (e.g., EC, EBRD, DFC).

- Development of industry and infrastructure: significant role in financing projects that support asset growth, environmental protection, efficiency, competitiveness, and energy security (including RES); governed by group-wide sector policies (Chemistry, Oil, Gas; Renewable Energy Sources; High Emission) introduced by the Credit Committee; 2025–2027 strategy targets >20% share in financing Poland’s energy transition, focusing on low-emission energy, emission-free vehicles, and low-emission buildings; Transition Plan approved Feb 24, 2025, sets actions for own operations (real estate emissions, low-emission/electric fleet) and financed emissions (pathways for energy production and residential real estate).
